english_translation: Live life to its fullest; Tempus fugit, utere.
Cultural_Context: A wisdom that has become a proverb about not caring about threats.

english_translation: Sticks to them like a shadow.
Cultural_Context: The proverb refers to someone who follows another person more than his shadow follows him.

english_translation: Kindness begets kindness.
Cultural_Context: It means that kindness and good treatment are the only way to gain people's love.

source_text: أحضر الناس جوابًا من لم يغضب
english_translation: If you stay calm, you are wise, but if you have a hot temper, you only show how stupid you are.
Cultural_Context: The proverb urges calm and patience, as anger can sometimes make a person miss the opportunity to answer or lead him to the wrong answer.

english_translation: pie in the sky.
Cultural_Context: This proverb describes the dreams of fools. It is also said: “Lighter than a bird's dream.”

english_translation: closer than one's shadow.
Cultural_Context: It means intense closeness, and it is quoted from the noble verse: “and We know what his soul whispers to him.”

english_translation: Much ado about nothing.
Cultural_Context: It is said about a man who talks a lot but does not work, and who makes promises but does not fulfill them.

english_translation: Much ado about nothing
Cultural_Context: Fawt: passed and went away. The proverb means literally: "I hear words and speech but I do not see action and implementation." It is said about someone who makes excuses but does not fulfill his promise. In the same meaning, it is said: "I hear the noise but I do not see the grinding".

english_translation: Runs like the wind.
Cultural_Context: The wind, in its fast blowing, is a metaphor for someone who raced and used his legs to quickly get away from a place of danger that he feared might overtake him or kill him.

english_translation: Experience is the best teacher
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that the experiences a person goes through make him learn and realize many situations in life.

english_translation: Action speaks louder than words
Cultural_Context: This proverb means that actions express intentions and sincerity more than words. It indicates that what a person does is more important and valuable than what he says, as actions reveal the true intention of people.

english_translation: Be old hat. / It’s as old as the hills.
Cultural_Context: A proverb used by Arabs to describe something old or someone who has lived a long time. In other words, it refers to something that has been around for a long time and has become outdated or unfashionable.

english_translation: A man of quick temper acts foolishly.
Cultural_Context: This proverb means that when a person gets angry, they lose control of themselves and act irrationally, but when they calm down, they feel regret for their previous actions and wish they had acted better. This proverb highlights the importance of calmness and thinking before taking any action.

source_text: إذا أنت أكرمت الكريم ملكته وإن أنت أكرمت اللئيم تمردا
english_translation: Never trust on unknown hands, you will never know how they stand by you and back stab with their brains.
Cultural_Context: It is a verse of poetry by Al-Mutanabbi means: If you do good to someone who is not good, he will be ungrateful for your blessings and will not thank you for your kindness to him.

english_translation: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means adapting to your environment, and not deviating from the customs and traditions of the people.

source_text: إذا ذكرت الذئب فأعد له العصا.
english_translation: when you speak of the storm, ready your sails
Cultural_Context: The proverb urges us to be well prepared for things and not to be negligent.

english_translation: when you speak of the storm, ready your sails
Cultural_Context: The proverb urges us to be well prepared for things and not to be negligent.

source_text: إذا رأيتَ أنيابَ الليثِ بارزة، فلا تَظُننَّ أنَّ الليثَ يبتسمُ
english_translation: Don't judge a book by its cover.
Cultural_Context: This proverb means that when you see warning or danger signs, you should not think them a sign of kindness. The idea is that protruding fangs are a signal of danger or threat, not a sign of a smile or greeting.

source_text: إذا كَانَ الكَلَامُ مِن فِضَّة فالسُكُوت مِن ذَهَب
english_translation: Speech is silver, silence is golden
Cultural_Context: A proverb shows the importance of silence compared to useless and meaningless talk.

english_translation: Make hay while the sun shines.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is quoted from a line of poetry, urging people to seize opportunities if they are available. The Arabs used to rely on this proverb in sorting out crops and grains such as barley and wheat, as they relied on the winds to separate the wheat from the straw. Just as sailors relied on the winds and their directions in order to move their sailing ships, these ships were a means for them to move between countries, and were not a means of luxury and comfort.

english_translation: I dug my own grave.
Cultural_Context: A short phrase that means I strove with all my will to an end that I discovered I had chosen for myself.

english_translation: Little enemies and little wounds must not be despised
Cultural_Context: "Do not belittle a small person in a quarrel... A mosquito can bleed a lion's eye." This is a popular proverb that means not to underestimate your enemy or anyone you are in a quarrel with, because a mosquito is the smallest insect in size, but it can sting the lion's eyeball and make it bleed severely, and the lion, with all its strength, cannot do anything to it or harm it at all. There is a verse in the Quran that indicates the same meaning, when God Almighty said, meaning that if a fly takes something from someone, he can never get it back. So, your enemy may have a high ability to harm you and you do not know, so do not belittle anyone, no matter how weak he appears to you.

english_translation: the destiny of a coward comes from over him.
Cultural_Context: The proverb indicates that a coward dies faster than a brave man, because death comes to him from where he has no defense. The proverb is used to show the uselessness of caution in the face of fate.

english_translation: Birds of a feather flock together.
Cultural_Context: It is a popular and common proverb, used to express the extent to which two people are similar or close in their actions or way of thinking and their compatibility with each other. The phrase has been used in some form since the mid-16th century, and a version of this phrase appeared in 1545 in a satire by the writer William Turner, who used a sentence from this proverb in his satirical comedy, On the Gentle Catholic, and the Rescue of the Romish Fox, in which he said: "Birds of one kind and colour always fly in one flock", the phrase was slightly different than it is today, but the main meaning is the same.

source_text: إن كان لك عند الكلب حاجة قل له يا سيدي.
english_translation: Call the bear “uncle” till, you are safe across the bridge.
Cultural_Context: This phrase is often used by some people to encourage using any means necessary to achieve a goal or objective, even if the methods are low or dishonorable.

english_translation: Every cloud has a silver lining.
Cultural_Context: It means that after difficulties and problems comes relief and ease. This proverb is used to encourage people to be patient and endure the difficult times, as relief will come later.

source_text: إنك لا تجني من الشوك العنب
english_translation: You can't make a silk purse out of a sow's ear.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used for someone who does good to the wrong people and for someone who tries to reform an abnormal person but to no avail in all his attempts.

english_translation: Take the will for the deed.
Cultural_Context: It means that the value of actions depends on the intention of the person who does them. The intention behind the action is what determines its value and impact, not just the action itself.

source_text: اتَّكَلْنا منه على خُصٍّ الاتحاد قوة
english_translation: Unity is strength.
Cultural_Context: When Aktham bin Al-Saifi Al-Tamimi felt his death was approaching, he called his sons, gave them a bundle of sticks, and asked each one of them to break it into small and separate pieces. No one, no matter how strong, could break the bundle while it was together. So the father took the bundle and separated it from each other, then gave it to his sons, and gave it to them to break it again while it was separate. They found it easy to break it, and each one of them was able to break it without any effort. He said to them: "My sons, there is strength in unity, and your coming together will make all your enemies unable to break you, just as you were unable to break these sticks together. Division is weakness and disagreement is destruction. A person is like a stick, if he unites with others, he becomes strong and powerful. Perhaps the weak who unite are better than the strong who separate, for one of you is weak on his own but strong with his brother." These were the best words of his.

source_text: احذر عدوّك مرّة وصديقك ألف مرّة، فإن انقلب الصّديق فهو أعلم بالمضرّة
english_translation: Better to have an enemy who slaps you in the face than a friend who stabs you in the back.
Cultural_Context: When a friend turns into an enemy, his stabs become more painful than the enemy's stabs. Your enemy's stab may be hurtful, but a friend knows your weak point and will direct one stab that will be fatal.

english_translation: A penny saved is a penny earned.
Cultural_Context: It is a popular proverb used to emphasize the need to save and avoid extravagance.

english_translation: Things got chaotic.
Cultural_Context: There was confusion among them, and the hunter with arrows could not be distinguished from the hunter with ropes.

english_translation: Speak well of the dead.
Cultural_Context: It is better to keep in mind the positive and good actions that the deceased did, rather than focusing on their faults or negative actions. This proverb encourages us to maintain respect and appreciation for the deceased and not to say things that might harm their memory.

source_text: ازرع جمیلًا ولو في غیر موضعه، فلن یضیع جمیل أینما زرعا
english_translation: A good deed is never lost.
Cultural_Context: Do good deeds everywhere, and do not belittle any good deed, even if it is not great, for you will find that one day in your life, the lives of your children, and family after, and it will not be lost in this world or in the hereafter.

source_text: اضرب حديدًا حاميًا لا نفع منه أن يبرد
english_translation: Strike while the iron is hot.
Cultural_Context: The proverb indicates the importance of acting quickly when circumstances are available.

source_text: اطلبوا العلم من المهد إلى اللحد
english_translation: Learn from the cradle to the grave.
Cultural_Context: Our noble Prophet commands us in this saying to learn and seek knowledge from the time we are born (from the cradle) until we die (to the grave).

english_translation: Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding.
Cultural_Context: A man came to our beloved Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he had a she-camel with him. He asked the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, for advice: "Should I leave my she-camel without tying it? Or should I tie it up to prevent it from moving and getting lost, and then put my trust in Allah?" The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, responded eloquently: "Tie it up and put your trust in Allah."

english_translation: Charity begins at home.
Cultural_Context: Priority is to support and help those close to you, because they deserve it more.

english_translation: All is well that ends well.
Cultural_Context: Things depend on their results and consequences.

english_translation: If you humble yourself too much, you will get trampled on.
Cultural_Context: It means that appearing too humble can demean a person and make him vulnerable to humiliation.

english_translation: A fault confessed is half redressed.
Cultural_Context: Admitting mistakes and guilt is a noble and virtuous behavior. The proverb indicates that courage and honesty in facing mistakes and learning from them are valuable manners, and are considered as a moral maturity.

english_translation: A bribe works like magic.
Cultural_Context: It is used to describe giving bribes and gifts to achieve what one wants.

source_text: التأني من الرحمن والعجلة من الشيطان.
english_translation: haste makes waste.
Cultural_Context: The proverb refers to the importance of taking things slowly and carefully to get better results.

english_translation: A bad neighbor is a misfortune, as much as a good one is a great blessing.
Cultural_Context: This proverb has Arab origins, as it is repeated in many Arab countries, especially Egypt, and Egyptians say, "Choose your neighbor before your house." There is a story behind this proverb. It goes back to a man who was a neighbor of Abu Daf Al-Baghdadi. This man's need became severe and his debts increased, so he had no choice but to sell his house. He actually put his house up for sale for 1,000 dinars, while his house was valued at only 500 dinars, and this is what most of his neighbors told him. When Abu Daf Al-Baghdadi repeated the information that the house was valued at 500 dinars, he said to him, "I am selling the house for 500 dinars, and the neighbors for 500 dinars." Abu Daf Al-Baghdadi was surprised by his response, so he offered him help and assistance and paid off his debts. The man confirmed that when he bought his house 20 years ago, he was thinking about the neighborhood with whom he had a brotherly and friendly relationship and found them to be of good origin. When his sons got married and left him, he refused to leave his friendship and neighborhood, which he saw as valuable to him as much as the value of his house.

english_translation: Necessity is the mother of invention.
Cultural_Context: It states that the primary driving force for most new inventions is a need.

english_translation: Love is blind
Cultural_Context: Love can be so emotional that it affects a person's ability to think rationally.

english_translation: But remember that good intentions pave many roads. Not all of them lead to hell.
Cultural_Context: Someone who directs or helps others to do a good deed is considered as if he had done the deed himself. The person who directs others to do a good deed is rewarded as much as the person who did the deed.

english_translation: let's call it a night.
Cultural_Context: Whatever you do in the morning will bring you profit and benefit, and it is proverb describes preferring to do something in the morning rather than in the evening.

source_text: الصحة تاج على رؤوس الأصحاء لا یراه إلا المرضى.
english_translation: Health is not valued till sickness comes.
Cultural_Context: It means that health is a great blessing and a precious treasure, but healthy people may not fully appreciate it. They do not realize its real value until they face health problems or get sick, and they become more aware of the importance of the health they had without noticing its value.

english_translation: A friend in need is a friend indeed.
Cultural_Context:
There was a man who advised his son to choose his friends carefully and to be close to only one and stay away from the rest because they are of no use to him when he needs them, but the son refused and defended them, saying, "My friends are loyal like your friends, father."

The father decided to test his son's friends to prove that he is true, so he asked him to slaughter a sheep and stain the ground with blood. He went to his son's first friend at night and knocked on the door. He came out and greeted him, and the father said, "The son of your friend's neighbor had a quarrel with your friend, and killed him. We want you to come with us to look into the matter." He said, "He is not my friend, and I do not know him." And so on until the last of his friends.

The father asked his son to go to his friends and tell them what happened, because they were all his father's friends. They all came to the house, and when they entered, they said, "Where is the dead man?" Then he took them into the dining room and found a cooked sheep!

The friends got angry and said, "This is a test for us," and he said, "No, but it is a lesson for my son, so that he may know that "a friend in need is a friend indeed." This proverb is repeated to this day.

english_translation: What is bred in the bone cannot come out of the flesh.
Cultural_Context: It means that the fact that a person has two types of characteristics; characteristics that are inherent in him and others that are acquired. The first of these cannot be changed, and if it is changed, the change is very difficult, and it is the nature. It is not a necessary that these characteristics are positive or negative. For example: generosity, kindness, good origin, goodness, and the person being one-faced with all people.

english_translation: Birds of feather flock together
Cultural_Context: The proverb expresses that the connection between people in life is not random, as good pmen are for good women and bad men are for bad women.

english_translation: A good Jack makes a good Jill.
Cultural_Context: It suggests that people with good morals and good intentions attract and deserve each other in social or personal relationships.

english_translation: A sound mind in a sound body.
Cultural_Context: It indicates that body care, good nutrition and exercise contribute to improving mental and intellectual abilities.

english_translation: Knowledge is power.
Cultural_Context: Knowledge and science give power and the ability to influence. An educated person has tools and resources that help him achieve his goals and face challenges, while ignorance restricts him and limits his ability to progress and influence.

english_translation: The end justifies the means
Cultural_Context: If the goal is big and important, the method used to achieve it, even if it is not ideal, is allowed.

english_translation: The last straw.
Cultural_Context: This proverb expresses how a simple event or small problem can lead to the collapse of something greater.

english_translation: Enough is as good as a feast.
Cultural_Context: It indicates that contentment and satisfaction with the blessings you have brings more happiness and reassurance than looking forward to what you do not have.

english_translation: English equivalent is actually the opposite meaning: never judge a book by its cover.
Cultural_Context: It means that we can judge people by their appearance or the way they deal with and talk. It is as if we know their secrets and what is in their hearts. This is contrary to what we have experienced in our lives and our dealings with people and situations.

english_translation: A word to a wise man is enough.
Cultural_Context: The intelligent person understands quickly and does not need much explanation and clarification, to the point that he can understand the matter by hand hint and other things without speaking.

english_translation: A man is known by the company he keeps.
Cultural_Context: Choosing the right friends is important because it affects an individual's behavior and beliefs.

english_translation: An evil chance seldom comes alone.
Cultural_Context: Hard times may come and go, making them more difficult to deal with.

english_translation: No flying from fate.
Cultural_Context: The proverb indicates that no one can prevent the destiny, as everyone has a destiny in this life that is written for him and he cannot change it.

english_translation: Forbidden fruit is the sweetest.
Cultural_Context: Prohibition may increase people's desire to obtain or experience the forbidden thing.

english_translation: Cleanliness is next to godliness.
Cultural_Context: A wisdom that urges cleanliness and that a person’s cleanliness reflects his faith.

english_translation: calm before the storm.
Cultural_Context: It means that there is a period of stillness or calm before a major event or upcoming crisis occurs.

english_translation: It is better to be alone than in bad company
Cultural_Context: Abu Ubaid said that this is one of their common proverbs in ancient and modern times.

source_text: الوقاية خير من العلاج/ درهم وقاية خير من قنطار علاج
english_translation: Prevention is better than cure
Cultural_Context: Taking preventive measures and procedures to avoid problems or diseases is much better than waiting until the problem occurs and then trying to treat it.

source_text: الوقتُ كالسَّيْفِ إن لم تَقْطعهُ قَطَعَك.
english_translation: Time is money
Cultural_Context: Time is like a sword, because it can be a useful tool if you use it right, or it can hurt you if you neglect it.

english_translation: to become unbearable
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to express that a situation has reached the point of extreme aggravation or distress, and cannot be tolerated any longer.

english_translation: Between the upper and nether millstone.
Cultural_Context: It means that a person or situation is in difficult circumstances and is confused about two difficult choices, where there is no easy way out. It refers to having to deal with pressure or challenges from two different or opposing sides.

source_text: تجري الرياح بما لا تشتهي السّفن
english_translation: Things don’t always go as they’re planned.
Cultural_Context: This is a line from a verse by Al-Mutanabbi, which is a metaphor means that life does not always go according to one’s desires.

english_translation: Address people in the language they can understand.
Cultural_Context: It means that communication with people should be done according to their level of understanding and intellect.

english_translation: For the LORD gives wisdom; from his mouth come knowledge and understanding.
Cultural_Context: Wisdom and advice are taken from someone who has been in the same situation.

english_translation: The sooner, the better
Cultural_Context: The proverb refers to the importance of doing good quickly and not postponing it.

english_translation: Less is more.
Cultural_Context: It is an equivalent for the popular proverb, “If speech is silver, then silence is gold.” This proverb and wisdom were used in many situations where people prolong their speech without benefit or advantage. It was also used to give advice to children and teach them the principles of public speaking and sobriety.

english_translation: Everything in moderation.
Cultural_Context: It is used to urge us to be economical. An Arab said to Al-Hasan Al-Basri: Teach me a moderate religion, neither going too far nor falling too low. He said: Well done, O Arab. The best things are the middle ones.

english_translation: Strike while the iron is hot.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means hurry up to accomplish what is asked of you without delay or slowing down. For example, when the required work is postponed, a person may lose an important opportunity that was destined for him, or it may become more difficult to implement what is required of him. This is like striking iron when it is hot, so it becomes easier to bend and shape it.

english_translation: Your brother from another mother.
Cultural_Context: This proverb describes a loyal friend who is like a brother not born of our mother. The story behind it has nothing to do with loyalty. According to the story, Luqman the Wise passed by a tent and found a woman sitting with a man. He asked her for a drink, so she gave him some to drink. Then he saw a child crying without anyone caring about him, so he asked who this child was. She replied that he belonged to her husband. He asked her about the man sitting with her, and she replied that he was her brother. He said, “There may be a brother you have whom your mother did not give birth to.” What he meant by that was that he realized that this man was not her brother and left the house.

source_text: رحم الله امرءًا عرف قدر نفسه.
english_translation: Cut your coat according to your cloth.
Cultural_Context: It indicates the importance of a person being realistic and knowing the limits of his abilities and ambitions without bragging or overestimating.

english_translation: What goes around comes around.
Cultural_Context: Anyone who participates in a work must get his share of it. If this work or cooking is poisonous, the cook may forget and taste it.

source_text: عاد بخفي حُنَيْن / عاد خالي الوفاض
english_translation: Cut off without a penny
Cultural_Context: Hunayn, a cobbler from Al-Hirah, was angered when a Bedouin haggled over a pair of shoes and then left without buying them. To teach him a lesson, Hunayn placed one shoe on a tree and another along the Bedouin's path. When the Bedouin dismounted to collect the shoes, Hunayn stole his camel and fled. The Bedouin returned to his people with only the shoes, leading to the saying "I brought you Hunayn's shoes," used to describe returning empty-handed and disappointed.

english_translation: Old habits die hard.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used when someone gives up a habit, generally bad, and then returns to it again. There are many stories behind it, but the most common one is about Halima, the wife of Hatim al-Ta'i, who was famous for his generosity. She was known for her extreme stinginess. She used to put very small amounts of ghee when cooking, and her husband told her that the ancients used to say that every time a woman put a spoonful of ghee in a cooking pot, Allah would extend her life by a day. So she started adding more spoonfuls of ghee to her cooking. But after a while, her only son died, so she wished for death and started adding less ghee to shorten her life. People said: Halima has returned to her old habit.

source_text: عامل الناس كما تحب أن تُعامَل.
english_translation: Do as you would be done.
Cultural_Context: This proverb encourages empathy and mutual respect, and urges behavior in ways that make human relationships more positive and polite.

source_text: عُصْفُورٌ باليَدّ خيرٌ من عشرة على الشجرة.
english_translation: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
Cultural_Context: An old popular proverb that is said to indicate the importance of doing things that have guaranteed results, even if they do not involve great benefits, instead of doing things that are not thought out and may not bring any benefit to the person, no matter how many potential benefits they may have.

english_translation: On pins and needles
Cultural_Context: It refers to a person who feels very tense or anxious and waiting nervously.

english_translation: In full swing.
Cultural_Context: It is used to refer to the effort put into carrying out a work or project quickly and efficiently.

english_translation: She digs her own grave.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is an ancient Arabic proverb. The story of a proverb: (Baraqish) is a dog that led the enemy soldiers to her family because of her barking. It was said (Baraqish has brought it upon its family.) and it was said (upon itself). This ancient popular proverb is used to describe someone who harms himself. It is an equivalent for: (He asked for it).

english_translation: Like the back of my hand
Cultural_Context: It means that the person knows something very well or has memorized it completely.

english_translation: A hungry stomach has no ears.
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to a person who loses all his mental strength when he is hungry, as all he is thinking about is how to get food, so he becomes weak and unable to speak or resist, and he uses force instead of reason.

english_translation: Divide and conquer
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to a strategy used to divide individuals or groups in order to gain control or benefit from the division.

english_translation: Unity is power.
Cultural_Context: When Aktham bin Al-Saifi Al-Tamimi felt his death was approaching, he called his sons, gave them a bundle of sticks, and asked each one of them to break it into small and separate pieces. No one, no matter how strong, could break the bundle while it was together. So the father took the bundle and separated it from each other, then gave it to his sons, and gave it to them to break it again while it was separate. They found it easy to break it, and each one of them was able to break it without any effort. He said to them: "My sons, there is strength in unity, and your coming together will make all your enemies unable to break you, just as you were unable to break these sticks together. Division is weakness and disagreement is destruction. A person is like a stick, if he unites with others, he becomes strong and powerful. Perhaps the weak who unite are better than the strong who separate, for one of you is weak on his own but strong with his brother." These were the best words of his.

source_text: في التأني السلامة وفي العجلة الندامة.
english_translation: Haste makes waste
Cultural_Context: It emphasizes the importance of thinking and taking time before acting to avoid mistakes and problems.

source_text: في الحب و الحرب كل وسیلة مشروعة.
english_translation: All is fair in love and war.
Cultural_Context: It is an expression of justification for using unusual or even dishonest methods to achieve desires in these special cases.

english_translation: Just around the corner.
Cultural_Context: Indicates that something or someone is very close to achieving their goal or reaching their desired status.

english_translation: Out of the frying-pan into the fire.
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to a person who escapes the heat of the scorching heat by taking refuge in the fire is like someone who escapes from a problem only to fall into an even more serious one.

english_translation: What's bred in the bone will come out in the flesh.
Cultural_Context: Everything comes out looking like the original.

english_translation: To err is human
Cultural_Context: It means that all humans make mistakes, and that making mistakes is part of human nature. It indicates that perfection is not possible for humans and that everyone makes mistakes from time to time.

english_translation: As you sow, so shall you reap.
Cultural_Context: It is used to encourage doing good.

source_text: لكل مقام مقال، لكل حادث حديث
english_translation: There is a time and place for everything.
Cultural_Context:
It means that every matter, action, or speech has a place that cannot be placed anywhere else. Ibn al-A'rabi recited:
Have mercy on me, may God guide you... For every situation there are suitable words
He said: It means be good to me so that I may remember you in every situation with your good deeds.

english_translation: Advice is ever in want.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that it is wise and sensible to seek advice from others in cases of uncertainty related to making a decision or embarking on a new experience or when confused about choosing between multiple options, as well as in the event of facing personal problems or even when facing conflicts in the work environment and other similar situations, as consultation increases the likelihood of reaching the prefect decision.

english_translation: One man’s meat is another man’s poison.
Cultural_Context: The problems or disturbances that your opponent or enemy suffer may be useful for you, as you can benefit from problems they have, so that you can make progress or outperform your opponent.

source_text: من تدخل فيما لا يعنيه، سمع ما لا يرضيه.
english_translation: keep your nose out of other people's business.
Cultural_Context: Interfering in the affairs of others is intended to find fault with people, and is religiously forbidden. Moreover, it is an immoral act. Your non-interference in the affairs of others is your duty, not a favor.

source_text: من خرج من داره قلَّ مقداره.
english_translation: East or west, home is best
Cultural_Context: This old Arabic proverb shows the importance of a person not imposing himself on others and not going to a place where he has no value. He should not be a burden on anyone, and this is what makes him be great for people and preserve his value and worth. Whoever imposes himself on others will not be valued by them.

english_translation: No pain, no gain.
Cultural_Context: The meaning of the proverb lies in working hard and diligence in order to achieve the desired wishes, and also that many sacrifices must be made and not surrender in the face of obstacles.

english_translation: you reap what you sow.
Cultural_Context: He got what he deserved.

english_translation: Add fuel to the fire.
Cultural_Context: It is said for those who make things more difficult and complicated.

english_translation: He laughs best who laughs last.
Cultural_Context: It is a proverb with a great motivational meaning that the end is for those who laugh last.

english_translation: No good deed goes unpunished.
Cultural_Context: It is said to punish good with evil. They say: “He was hit by a hand” if he slapped him in the face. There is a similar proverb: “The last service of the invaders was beating.”

english_translation: Let’s get everything out on the table.
Cultural_Context: This proverb emphasizes the full presence of all parties to an event.

english_translation: No such thing as a free lunch.
Cultural_Context: If there is something free does no harm, but it is considered booty; so take as much of it as you can.

english_translation: Every dog is a tiger in his own street.
Cultural_Context: No matter how lowly a person is despised in the eyes of others, he has pride in himself and his home that he feels.

english_translation: Like talking to a brick wall.
Cultural_Context: It is said about someone who deviates from the clear truth, even if he is told about an animal that it is a bull (i.e. a male bull), he says: Milk it, and the male is not milked.

english_translation: Gloom of night will lift and vanish
Cultural_Context: We have to endure the darkness of the night because it will soon end at the break of dawn.

source_text: إدي العيش لخبازه، ولو أكل نصه
english_translation: Never send a boy to do a man's job.
Cultural_Context: A person should seek the help of people with knowledge and experience, no matter what the cost; this is better than entrusting his projects or affairs to those who do not know (in order to save money), and then what he wants will end up being lost.

source_text: إذا كان الكلام من فضة فالسكوت من ذهب.
english_translation: Speech is silver, silence is gold.
Cultural_Context: It is said when talking about something that increases problems, then silence is better.

source_text: إذا كان حبيبك عسل ما تلحسوش كله
english_translation: Don't take advantage of a good thing.
Cultural_Context: It means if someone lets you do something, don't go any further.

source_text: إن عشقت اعشق قَمر، وإن سرقت اسرق جمل.
english_translation: Go big or go home.
Cultural_Context: If you are to be blamed for something, then do something so great that is worthy to be blamed.

source_text: إن غاب القط، العب يا الفار
english_translation: When the cat is away the mice will play.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to describe the chaos that occurs in the absence of officials.

english_translation: It takes two to tango.
Cultural_Context: People must work together to achieve success.

english_translation: Show me your green
Cultural_Context: Pay me the money, and I will be at your service.

english_translation: The apple doesn’t fall far from the tree.
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to someone's talent that is inherited from his father, or to praise both the son and the father. The story of the proverb: There was a goose that laid two eggs and died, so the owner of the goose took these two eggs and put them with the eggs of a hen so that they would hatch together, and after the eggs hatched, the two geese lived with the chickens. One day, the hen and her children approached a water basin, so the two geese jumped into the water and started swimming without any prior training, so the owner of the hen said, "The son of a goose is a swimmer."

source_text: ابنك زي ما تربيه، وجوزك زي ما تعوديه.
english_translation: The apple doesn’t fall far from the tree.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is used for someone who inherits certain skills from his parents, and as another proverb says, “This cub is from that lion.”

english_translation: A burnt child dreads the fire.
Cultural_Context: Meaning: He was trained in this craft in the heads of orphans, because they need to get a haircut without paying money, and none of them would object if he made a mistake. It is used for someone who take an advantage of the weak people to benefit him, even if it will harm them.

source_text: اِتْغَدَّى بُهْ قَبْلْ مَا يِتْعَشَّى بَكْ
english_translation: Get your blow in first.
Cultural_Context: Eat him before he eats you. It comes from the Arab proverb: “Eat a goat for lunch before it eats you for dinner.” It is used to encourage being firm. Among the proverbs of the modern generation mentioned in Majma’ al-Amthal with the same meaning is: “Catch the thief before he catches you.”

english_translation: Easy does it.
Cultural_Context: There are things that require patience and endurance, just as rice needs a very low flame to cook on.

english_translation: We are in the same boat.
Cultural_Context: It is a metaphorical expression that means that we are in the same situation.

source_text: اربُط الحمار مَطرح ما صاحبه عايز
english_translation: Obey orders, if you break owners.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said as a warning against not doing something without asking its owner, in order to be safe from the consequences. It means you have to implement the what is required without discussing it, because the donkey might be lost or stolen, so you will not be blamed.

english_translation: Experience is the best teacher.
Cultural_Context: The proverb shows the preference of someone who has tried something or gone through an experience over a doctor.

source_text: اسمع كلامك أصدقك أشوف أمورك استعجب
english_translation: Put your money where your mouth is.
Cultural_Context: It indicates a contradiction in actions that do not match what is said and a lack of honesty.

english_translation: Ease your mind.
Cultural_Context: It means not getting into an argument and giving your mind a break from getting into potentially trivial discussions.

english_translation: kill the chicken to scare the monkey.
Cultural_Context: If a person intends to do something and sees another person being beaten or humiliated for doing the same thing, he becomes terrified and does not do it for fear of being humiliated.

source_text: اطبخى يا جاريه كلِّف يا سيدي.
english_translation: If you pay peanuts you get monkeys.
Cultural_Context: The maid cannot cook unless her master brings her the ingredients to prepare the food. Meaning: Nothing comes from nothing or without preparation. It also means that you can make anything by money.

source_text: اقلب القدرة على فُمها تطلع البنت لأمها
english_translation: Like mother like daughter.
Cultural_Context: It means that nature prevails over nurture in women, even if a woman practices behavior that is different from her mother, she will have the same characteristics as her mother.

source_text: اكل مسني واعيش مهني، ولا كبابك اللي قتلني/ لاقيني ولا تغديني.
english_translation: A civil denial is better than a rude grant.
Cultural_Context: A little food with peace of mind is better than the best food with humiliation or harm.

english_translation: Defend your home.
Cultural_Context: Defend your land.

source_text: الإبرة اللي فيها خيطين ما تخيطش
english_translation: Two cooks spoil the broth.
Cultural_Context: Because a needle is so fine that only one thread can go into a garment. A matter that depends on two things cannot be completed, because they may differ. Similar to this is the proverb: “A ship that has two captains will sink.”

english_translation: There’s always a next time.
Cultural_Context: It is said by someone who is trying to convince another person that he will satisfy him next time, whether in an invitation, paying money, or in anything else.

english_translation: A hungry belly has no ears.
Cultural_Context: Severe hunger may lead some people to disbelief, disobedience, and abandonment of acts of obedience.

english_translation:
-There’s always a catch.
-You don’t get something for nothing.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said for someone who expects something good from evil people, such as a gift from a miser, a trust from a thief, or a free gift from someone whose only intention is always to make a profit.

english_translation: Unwillingness easily finds an excuse.
Cultural_Context: The smart person is the one who can succeed with the least possible means, and makes use of what he has, no matter how little, to achieve his goal. The proverb literally means that a smart woman can spin fabric even using a donkey's leg.

english_translation: Blood is thicker than water
Cultural_Context: It indicates that kinship cannot be abandoned.

source_text: العبد في التفكير والرب في التدبير.
english_translation: man proposes and god disposes
Cultural_Context: A person should think about solving his problems with all his strength, and Allah is the source of success. The proverb points that a person should not worry about problems and tire himself out thinking, while Allah has already provided a solution for them.

english_translation: haste makes waste.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to encourage patience, thinking, and not rushing, because some things do not get enough study and deep thinking.

english_translation:
Too much ado about nothing.
Much bran and little meal.
Cultural_Context: People cry so hard when the dead person is just a dog. The proverb is said when something is advertised in an exaggerated way while in reality it is very small.

english_translation: You get what you pay for
Cultural_Context: An expensive thing is worth the price because of its quality. This proverb advises buying a good, well-crafted thing, no matter how expensive it is; it is better than a cheap, poor thing that a person might throw away half of because it is not good.

english_translation: The absent party is not so faulty.
Cultural_Context: Do not blame a person for his absence; he may have an excuse or a reason to justify this absence; it is better to wait until his excuse is heard.

english_translation: Beauty’s in the eye of the beholder.
Cultural_Context: The origin of this proverb, as narrated in "Aesop's Fables," goes back to a beauty contest organized by Jupiter, one of the Roman gods. Jupiter sat on his throne as the beautiful animals paraded before him one by one, showing off their beauty. The peacock and its chick passed by, followed by the giraffe and its calf, and so on. Just before Jupiter could announce his judgment and declare the winning animal, a monkey ran in front of him, proudly, showing off her baby. All the attendees burst into laughter and tried to persuade the monkey to withdraw from the contest, but she refused, insisting that her baby was the most beautiful of all the animals. Jupiter laughed and said, "The monkey's child is a gazelle in its mother's eyes."

source_text: القرش الأبيض ينفع في اليوم الأسود.
english_translation: To lay by for a rainy day.
Cultural_Context: A penny is one hundredth of the Egyptian pound and was minted from aluminum, so it was white in color. It can be saved for a bad day. A person should save some of their money or earnings for times of hardship.

english_translation: Many hands make light work.
Cultural_Context: It is a metaphor for cooperation and highlighting this good quality.

english_translation: Strength in numbers.
Cultural_Context: Al-Kitrah: abundance. It was said in the past: “Two weak ones overcome one strong one.”

english_translation: Lies don't last.
Cultural_Context: It means that the lie has no legs to walk with, and refers to the fact that the lies will be revealed soon. Some people say "falsehood” instead of lying. This expression is used in the opposite meaning also: “The thief has no legs.”, as it means that the thief does not have two legs to stand on, but rather he quickly flees.

english_translation: A lion at home, a lamb abroad.
Cultural_Context: This proverb describes someone who shows his strength in his home, no matter how weak he is.

source_text: اللي اتلسع من الشوربه، ينفخ في الزبادي.
english_translation: Once bitten, twice shy.
Cultural_Context: It is said about someone who has a bad experience with something, so he doubts everything similar to it.

source_text: اللي يتلسع من التعبان يخاف من الحبل
english_translation: Once bitten, twice shy.
Cultural_Context: It is said about someone who has a bad experience with something, so he doubts everything similar to it.

source_text: اللي إيدُه في المَيَّة مِش زَيّ اللي إيدُه في النار
english_translation: Easier said than done.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is popular in Egypt, as it refers to the privacy of pain and no one feels the pain except the one in pain. This proverb is said in the ocassion of relatives ask the person in pain to be patient ot forgive.

source_text: اللي خدته القرعة، تاخده ام الشعور
english_translation: What goes around comes around.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is often said by a woman when she finds out that her husband is in a relationship with another woman or intends to marry another woman. She says this proverb as a metaphor for the fact that she this man has many faults and that the one will marry him will be oppressed ad suffer like her.

source_text: اللي عَلى راسُه بَطحَة يِحَسِّس عَليها
english_translation: If the cap fits, wear it.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that the guilty person, no matter how small or great his sin or violation is, thinks that the words are directed at him, even if they are useless, and always feels himself suspected, and revolves around his action when anyone mentions a subject or a violation that he may have committed and was not revealed.

english_translation: Half of the world not know how the other half lives.
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to people who do not know the real issue and interfere in it without being aware of it.

source_text: اللي مالكش فيه، مالكش دعوة بيه:
english_translation: Mind your own business.
Cultural_Context: A person should not interfere in what does not concern him, nor should he interfere in the affairs of others, their news, their secrets, or their actions.

source_text: اللي مايطول العنب حامض عنه يقول.
english_translation: A bad workman blames his tools.
Cultural_Context: Some people use this proverb to refer to people who blame circumstances and external factors for their failure, while this failure is due to the person’s lack of enthusiasm and the lack of effort he exerts to reach his goal or objective.

source_text: اللي يعوزه البيت يحرم على الجامع
english_translation: Charity begins at home.
Cultural_Context: that reflects practical cultural values aligned with religious commands, urging Muslims to prioritize according to the requirements of wisdom.

english_translation: The hole calls the thief
Cultural_Context: It means that a person should protect what they own and not leave it in a situation that encourages theft or loss, thereby being responsible for losing them.

source_text: المنحوس منحوس لو علقنا علي رأسه فانوس
english_translation: A bad penny always comes back.
Cultural_Context:
The unlucky person is always unlucky no matter what he does.
It is said about someone who is pursued by bad luck wherever he goes.
This sentence is said about a person who is pursued by bad luck and is deprived of luck. The story goes back to two brothers, one of whom is rich and the other is poor. One day, the rich man decided to send money to his brother indirectly, so as not to embarrass him, so he threw a bundle of money in his way, and waited to know that he had found money on the road, but his brother told him that he had decided to come with his eyes closed that day, so the rich brother said: “The unlucky person will remain unlucky even if we hang a lantern on his head.”

english_translation: The proof's in the pudding.
Cultural_Context:
"If you claim to be a diver, then here is the water; prove it."
This proverb is said when people are uncertain about someone's expertise, so they put them to the test to verify their abilities, much like a diver being tested by diving into the sea.

english_translation: Touch wood.
Cultural_Context:
It is a proverb used by Egyptians and foreigners alike (touch wood), and it is said when praising the virtues of a person or thing, with the aim of protecting it from envy or harm. The expression has a Coptic origin, as the wood is the cross, because the word for the cross in the Coptic language is "shi athwaf" and means the holy wood, and the ancient Copts called for always holding on to the holy wood, claiming that it protects you from everything. The holy wood for them represents blessing and immunity from all evil, and therefore a person holding the wood means holding the cross and being blessed by it.
According to what was mentioned by the Greek Orthodox Patriarch Anastasios Zavalis, during the reign of Emperor Constantine it was customary for Christian believers to walk in public processions and touch the wooden cross with the aim of obtaining blessing and healing and touching it three times according to the doctrine of the Trinity (Father, Son, Holy Spirit).
After the placement of the central wooden cross in Constantinople, it became a tradition to touch any wooden cross for blessing, then the custom later changed to touching anything made of wood, to protect it from harm and injury.

source_text: امشي على مهلك، علشان توصل بسرعة
english_translation: Hold your horse, you will arrive quickly.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used especially for drivers who often have accidents that cause them to fail due to uncontrolled speed, and this proverb can also be used to warn against all harmful speed.

english_translation: It takes two to tango
Cultural_Context: One hand cannot clap; the other hand must join in. This proverb is used to illustrate the benefits of cooperation.

english_translation: where there is nothing the king loses his rights
Cultural_Context: It is said about a person who no one covets because he does not own anything or has no value. This proverb is used in response to someone who says, “Beware, there are those who covet him.”

english_translation: Apples and oranges.
Cultural_Context: Toukh and Melig are two villages in Egypt far from each other. It is said of someone who mixes up unrelated things in his speech and goes off topic.

english_translation: Apples and oranges.
Cultural_Context: It is surprising that a person with a different nature would form an alliance with a person with a completely different nature, and it is impossible for them to come together because of their different natures.

english_translation: The fox guarding the henhouse.
Cultural_Context: Meaning: The one who protects (the house or facility) is the one who steals from it. Interpretation: It is said when corruption (especially financial) spreads among those in power or positions.

english_translation: bluster one's way out
Cultural_Context: It refers to the person who starts shouting and accusing others to distract other people from defending themselves instead of thinking about accusing him.

english_translation: to be in deep water
Cultural_Context: Someone opened a Turkish bath and announced that entry to the bath was free. When the customers left the bath, the owner would seize their clothes and refuse to hand them back unless they paid. The customers would protest, saying: Didn't you say that entry to the bath was free? He would reply: Entering the bath isn't the same as leaving it.

english_translation: He was born with a silver spoon in his mouth.
Cultural_Context: Like a chicken that finds food under its feet while walking effortless. This proverb describes a person who finds sustenance in the things he does.

english_translation: In love with his own reflection.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used for someone who is proud of his appearance, his clothes, or his appearance and beauty, just as a peacock is proud of his long, colorful feathers.

english_translation: Give him an inch and he’ll take a mile.
Cultural_Context: We ignored his entry and acceptance into our house, so he entered with his donkey as well. This proverb describes someone who is greedy and oversteps his bounds when he is treated with leniency.

english_translation: What goes around comes around.
Cultural_Context: The one who cooks poison must taste it, whether for covet or otherwise. It is said of those who have some of their work, and of those who seek to harm people, they must suffer from their work, like a cook who forgets and tastes the poison he is making for others.

english_translation: He turns a blind eye.
Cultural_Context:
The origin of this proverb lies in the "Delta Train," which must pass through and stop at Banha regardless of its destination. This means that the first stop after Cairo is Banha. Passengers heading to Banha, who couldn’t find a seat, would often ask the seated passengers to let them sit for the short distance to Banha, which only takes a few minutes. Afterward, the Banha passengers would get off, and the "Bahari" (northern) passengers would return to their seats.

This led to a common trick among passengers traveling to farther provinces to secure seats. They would ask the seated passengers to let them sit by claiming they were only traveling as far as Banha. Since Banha is a station where many passengers disembark to catch other train lines, many people would exit the train, most of whom were not actually from Banha. Those who had given up their seats would find themselves sitting again but not in their original seats. Thus, the trick became common, and anyone who wanted to have a seat on a crowded train would "pretend to be from Banha."

source_text: عصفور في اليد خير من عشرة على الشجرة:
english_translation: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said in the context of greed and lack of contentment, and it can also be used in the opposite sense, i.e., acting with caution and fear of taking risks. There are many stories and tales behind this proverb, but the most commonly told one is about a person who had a bird in his hand. While walking, he saw a group of birds in a tree, he wanted them and let go of the bird in his hand and climbed the tree. As soon as he got close to them, they all flew away. Hence the proverb, "A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush."

english_translation: Small but mighty.
Cultural_Context: It describes anyone as small as an ant, yet he does a remarkable job. This proverb describes a great action that comes from a person who is young in age or position. It is similar to the proverb: “God's secret is placed in the weakest of his creation.”

english_translation: Abundance like want ruins many
Cultural_Context: Knowledge: Companionship and friendship. This proverb discusses that excess in something turns it into its opposite.

english_translation: (Clothes make the man.)
Cultural_Context: If you dress the stick well, it will turn into the most beautiful bride. It is said about a person who spends excessively on his appearance and clothes - or someone else spends on him - while he is a person who is the opposite of what his clothes show.

english_translation: (You can't make an omelet without breaking a few eggs.
Cultural_Context: This proverb signifies the true appreciation of life's beauty, which we only fully recognize after effort, struggle, fatigue, and hardship. It highlights that an achievement gains value in our lives when it is earned through hard work. If something comes easily and without effort, we are more likely to take it for granted and not feel the pain of losing it, as we did not work hard to obtain it. The proverb encourages perseverance and struggle to truly savor the sweetness of accomplishment.

english_translation: to make a mountain out of a molehill.
Cultural_Context: The term "الحبة" refers to a single grain of wheat or barley, meaning something small in size. On the other hand, "القبة" refers to a large silo used for storing grains, which is shaped like a dome, and some house roofs were also dome-shaped. This term signifies something large in size. The relationship between "القبة" and "الحبة" is one of contrast, akin to the relationship between small and large. This means that the person being referred to in the proverb exaggerates and magnifies things, surrounding them with a grandeur that is greater than their actual size, level, or value—similar to comparing a small grain to a large dome.

english_translation: Love is blind.
Cultural_Context: A lover does not see the faults of his beloved.

english_translation: Like it or lump it
Cultural_Context: The person says this phrase to his opponent who threatens him with punishment associated with the occurrence of the action.

english_translation: It’s ill sitting at Rome and striving with the pope.
Cultural_Context: When someone is warned not to overstep the bounds of a person of high status in society, he is told, “Be careful, not every bird is edible,” meaning that this person is not someone you can resist. People differ in their nature and constitution, just as birds differ in their nature, not all of them are edible. Likewise, people differ in their nature and are distinguished in their social status.

source_text: من كان بيته من زجاج، لا يقذف الناس بالحجارة
english_translation: People who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means if you threw a stone at someone and the stone came back to you, the whole house would collapse. This proverb is used for someone who talks about people's faults, while he is full of faults.

english_translation: every little helps
Cultural_Context: Sometimes it is something small and simple, but it is useful and can fix something big.

english_translation: Eating is his concern.
Cultural_Context: It is said to a person who eats voraciously.

source_text: يا خبر النهاردة بفلوس، بكرة يبقي ببلاش
english_translation: Let's wait and see.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used so that a person does not worry about hearing news, and does not make an effort or spend money to know it; because if he waits a little (until tomorrow), this news will be within the person’s reach, for free.

english_translation: I wish I have the patience of a saint.
Cultural_Context: Asking Allah to give man the patience of Job, peace be upon him, in the face of adversity

source_text: يا فَرْحَة ما تَمِّت خَدها الغُراب وطار.
english_translation: To rain on one’s parade.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is used when one is disappointed after a short-lived and intense joy.

english_translation: What a dead loss you are
Cultural_Context: A study on the behavior and lives of crows discovered that crows love all things that sparkle in the sun, and that each crow has its own secret storehouse, which could be a hole in a tree, under the roof of an old tower, or behind a stone on a bridge. One of the study team was able to reach one of the crows’ stores, and found in it a piece of a broken mirror, a cup handle, a piece of tin, another piece of metal, and other trivial things that have no value except that they sparkle in the sun. Hence the proverb “How much the crow brought to his mother” goes for anyone who buys or brings something that has no value or use.

english_translation: An old hand
Cultural_Context: It is used figuratively to describe someone who is battle-tested or seasoned in a particular field.

english_translation: Cave in. / He surrenders. / He admits defeat. / He gives up the fight.
Cultural_Context: The white banner is a symbol of surrender or giving up in a conflict or competition.

english_translation: No problem./ take it or leave it."
Cultural_Context: There is a popular proverb that says: “Between the seller and the buyer, God opens” – meaning that if the two agree, whether by acceptance or rejection, by mutual consent – ​​then there is no problem.

english_translation: He kills the victim and then shows up at the funeral.
Cultural_Context: It is said about someone who causes a problem, then comes to console the person who has the problem, and comforts him with kind words.

english_translation: Face the music. / To take the bull by the horns.
Cultural_Context: It is said to those who avoid problems that they should confront them and make decisive decisions about them.

english_translation: Old habits die hard.
Cultural_Context: It means that a flutist may die while his fingers keep playing. This expression refers to someone who is controlled by a habit that he cannot give up, regardless of the circumstances, even to the point of death.

english_translation: There is always more to learn.
Cultural_Context: Teacher refers to a master in their craft. It means that no matter how skilled the master or knowledgeable the scholar in his field, there’s always more to learn.

english_translation: small but mighty (or mighty mite)
Cultural_Context: This expression is used to describe a weak or simple person who unexpectedly turns out to be the one who solves the problem or brings about a good outcome.

english_translation: To reach a breaking point
Cultural_Context: The situation has become intolerable.

english_translation: To know which side one's bread is buttered on
Cultural_Context: This idiom describes a smart person who addresses issues by examining their origins, because eating the chuck is more challenging than eating consuming other cuts of meat.

english_translation: The shortest distance between two points is a straight line.
Cultural_Context: A popular Arabic proverb, quoted from the anecdotes of Juha. When he was asked, “Where is your ear, Juha?” he raised his right hand and circled it above his head, pointing to his left ear! The proverb is used for someone who leaves the shortest distances to reach his goal and goes to the furthest. It is also used for someone who talks too much or chatters.

source_text: أنت أمير وأنا أمير من يقود الحمير.
english_translation: Two kings can't rule a kingdom. / Too many cooks spoil the broth.
Cultural_Context: An Emirati proverb about people who think they are responsible for the entire work, but at the same time do not do their part. Work is everyone’s responsibility, and if he alone is responsible, who will do the rest of the work?

english_translation: When the tree is fallen, every one runs to it with his axe
Cultural_Context: The proverb is a metaphor for enemies who take advantage of the slightest opportunity of weakness in this person to attack his life or reputation.

source_text: إذا كان المتحدث مينون يكون المستمع عاقل
english_translation: Don't take everything at face value.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that speech must be rational, and not everything said should be taken at face value. If the speaker does not know what he is saying, it is better for the listener to be rational and critical.

english_translation: Roll with the punches.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that if life is not as you wish and all the people around you are against you, or the circumstances you are going through contain great changes that you are unable to change, so adapt to it. The proverb does not mean that you should go against the flow, but rather that you should adapt to it according to your ability to do so.

source_text: إذا ياتك العويه من السفية خلها.
english_translation: Don't give a fool a platform.
Cultural_Context: (عويه: wrong thing) If something bad happens to you from a fool, do not pay any attention to him. It is said when we want to prevent a person from responding to the one who harmed him.

source_text: إشلك بالبحر وأهواله، ورزق الله على السيف
english_translation: Don't reinvent the wheel.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said about a person who seeks hardships to reach a specific goal, and neglects the easy and available path for him.

english_translation: Old is gold.
Cultural_Context: It indicates the importance of respecting the past, especially the traditions and customs of the people.

english_translation: Be sane.
Cultural_Context: One of the proverbs that calls for reason.

english_translation: After black clouds, clear weather./ Slow and steady wins the race.
Cultural_Context: An indication that patience may be the key to overcoming challenges or difficulties.

source_text: اصبوعي في حلوجهم وصبوعهم في عيوني.
english_translation: Evil in return for god deed.
Cultural_Context: One of the popular proverbs that expresses the rejection of ingratitude. It means that there are those who do a lot of good and in return they only receive ingratitude.

english_translation: Do good and cast it into the sea.
Cultural_Context: It is used to encourage people to do good deeds, regardless of who deserves them or not.

english_translation: Contentment is wealth.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is an advice for people to be content with Allah's allottation for them, and they will feel like they are rich.

english_translation: The worst is yet to come.
Cultural_Context: (لاغش: an unusual movement of the wave). It indicates the existence of an action that will lead to a devastating disaster.

source_text: البحر له ناس لفيحه، يعرفون التوح من اليره، موب كل من تاح سريحه، قال هذا خيط وبيره.
english_translation: Never send a boy to do a man's job.
Cultural_Context: An Emirati proverb that is said to emphasize that every person has his own specialty, and every profession has its own experts and craftsmen.

source_text: البعد بعد القلوب موب بعد الدروب.
english_translation:
Love knows no distance.

or 

Distance means so little, when you mean so much.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said to someone who is not reassured about his loved ones and does not care about them due to the long distance. Therefore, the real distance is the distance from the heart and mind, not the distance from the land or place.

english_translation: You reap what you sow.
Cultural_Context: The meaning of the proverb is that when the seeds are planted, they produce good plants if the seed is good. If it is good, the crop will be good, but if it is bad, the crop will be affected and spoiled. This proverb shows the importance of raising children properly and bringing them up with good qualities, good values ​​and examples that are passed on from one generation to the next.

english_translation: Jealousy eats away at the jealous.
Cultural_Context: It indicates that the envious person lives in misery and does not gain any good from envy.

english_translation: A pint-sized man.
Cultural_Context: The proverb shows that a boy's manliness and chivalry are evident from a young age, and people understand his movements, and hopes are attached to him, so he is treated like a man.

english_translation: If everything perishes, a loyal friend will remain.
Cultural_Context: It means that material things will inevitably pass away, but a loyal friend will remain.

english_translation: The rotten apple injures its neighbor.
Cultural_Context: This proverb warns against associating with fools and the dishonorable.

english_translation: still waters run deep.
Cultural_Context: This Emirati proverb is said when you see a person with a good appearance and you admire him and get a positive impression of him, while he is bad in character and work.

english_translation:
The axe forgets but the tree remembers.
or
The tree remembers what the axe forgets.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said when someone who hurts another person may have a good relationship with him. The one who hurts may forget his wrongdoing, but the one who was hurt cannot forget it.

english_translation: Choose a partner/ friend before choosing a path.
Cultural_Context: It shows the importance of a friend.

english_translation: Don't beat a dead horse.
Cultural_Context: There is no point in hitting and insulting someone who does not feel or feel pain, he is like a dead person, so hitting and talking to him is useless.

english_translation: the eyes desire what the hands can't reach.
Cultural_Context: It indicates that the speaker is talking about his experience and knowledge of things, but the little money or management he has in his hand hides his ability and good conduct.

english_translation: Curiosity killed the cat.
Cultural_Context: This proverb calls for staying away from curiosity, and it goes back to a story about an old woman who died because of her curiosity.

english_translation: You can't teach an old dog new tricks.
Cultural_Context: The meaning of this proverb is that a corrupt adult who has reached adulthood is difficult to re-educated.

english_translation: Lies will get found out.
Cultural_Context: It indicates that lies are usually eventually exposed, and have limited or short-lived impact.

source_text: الكلب ما ينبح الا عند دار أهله
english_translation: The dog only barks at its owner's house.
Cultural_Context: A sign of the dog's loyalty and appreciation for those who take care of it

english_translation: let bygones be bygones.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is effective psychological advice for those whose thinking is mortgaged to the past, which is a serious psychological illness because it harms sound thinking and paralyzes a person’s movement towards the future. Thinking makes a person become a prisoner of the past and its bitter memories, and makes him cry over the ruins of those who have passed away, but the tear that falls will not return, and this proverb spreads a spirit of optimism and a new start.

english_translation: Let's wait and hold to see what the future holds.
Cultural_Context: It indicates that the news that is currently hidden will be revealed with time, and it is similar to the Levantine proverb “Tomorrow the snow will melt and the meadow will appear.”

source_text: اللي في قلبه صلاة ما تفوته.
english_translation:
The key to success is to focus on goals, not obstacles.
\ Don’t wait for opportunity, Create it.
Cultural_Context: Whoever wants something will strive for it, and circumstances will not make him forget his goals.

source_text: اللي ما عنده عمل يكاري له جمل واللي ما عنده حيله يلعب التيله
english_translation: A cat in gloves catches no mice.
Cultural_Context: One of the proverbs that calls for work and staying away from idleness and unemployment.

source_text: اللي ما له أول ما له تالي.
english_translation: Without a past, there is no present.
Cultural_Context: A popular Emirati proverb used to emphasize that he who has no past has no present, and Emirati citizens should be proud of the past that brought them to this present.

english_translation: No beginning, no end.
Cultural_Context: (تفر) is the stern of the ship and (صدر) is the front of the ship. The meaning of this proverb is that everything has a beginning and an end.

english_translation: Like father like son.
Cultural_Context: One of the popular proverbs in the UAE about children being dutiful to their parents, and that everything returns to a person, if he obeys his parents he will grow up, and then his children will obey him.

source_text: المطر قطرة على قطرة يظول غدير.
english_translation: A journey of thousand miles begins with a single step.
Cultural_Context: Repetition and consistency can create great success or impact over time, just as every raindrop contributes to a pond or stream.

source_text: اليوز لو ما تكسره ما تاكل لبه
english_translation: Nothing ventured, nothing gained./ Whoever strives shall find, whoever sows shall reap.
Cultural_Context: اليوز: walnut, the letter jim is reversed, لبه: the fruit. It means that reaching the goal requires effort, fatigue, and strength in order to obtain it.

source_text: انفخ يا شريم قال برطم ما هست
english_translation: Born to suffer./ You can not escape bad luck
Cultural_Context: (برطم: lip), (شريم: the person with a cleft lip). The proverb means that the person with cleft lips cannot blow, and this proverb is used to describe a person who wishes for something but does not get it because of obstacles.

english_translation: Gild the lily.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used when the results are contrary to expectations. There are many things started as a joke and then became a reality. The pranks and incidents on this matter are too numerous to count.

english_translation: Gild the lily.
Cultural_Context: Such as saying: make matters worse, or pour oil on the fire. The proverb refers to a person who wants to fix something but accidentally destroys it. It is said that the story of this proverb is a fairy tale that goes back to a dog who wanted to put kohl in his eye and put his claws in it.

source_text: بو طبيع ما ايوز عن طبعه (ايوز: يبتعد)
english_translation: Old habits die hard.
Cultural_Context: It indicates that every person has a trait that is difficult for him to get rid of, and it is often used as an example of bad traits.

english_translation: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
Cultural_Context: It is a principle in life that calls for realism in dealing and avoiding illusions and dreams, and building on what actually exists, not what is present in the imagination. So, one should not chase after a mirage. What a person is like in his present is what will determine his future. As they say in political culture: (Take and demand), and in social culture (A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush).

english_translation: A good neighbor adds value to your house.
Cultural_Context: The proverb urges to choose a good friend.

english_translation: Have the luck of the devil
Cultural_Context: It indicates that the person has good luck.

english_translation: Birds of a feather flock together.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that it is better for a person to be with who is of the same origin, whether in marriage, work, or otherwise.

english_translation: A kind word is like a spring day.
Cultural_Context: The proverb calls for saying kind words and avoiding harsh words so that people do not turn away from you.

english_translation: render good for evil.
Cultural_Context: "Sheena": a bad deed, and "zina": a good deed. This Emirati proverb is used to emphasize responding to bad with good and harm with kindness.

english_translation: Old habits die hard
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said to a person who gave up a habit and then returned to it again.

english_translation: keep your nose out of other people's business.
Cultural_Context: Rain falling in a remote area does not benefit its residents. It is better not to think about it. The point is that each person should take care of his personal affairs and not care about and think about what others suffer. In other words, only take care of your affairs and do not interfere in the affairs of others.

english_translation: Bury the hatchet.
Cultural_Context: It means that the difficulty has been removed between a group of people. It is said of disputing parties who have reconciled after a disagreement.

english_translation: Eida knows Saeeda.
Cultural_Context: A popular proverb about marriage, that whoever wants to find a wife, asks a woman to do it because she knows othe women best. In the proverb, "Eida" is a famous matchmaker in the Emirate of Abu Dhabi.

english_translation: Lost is the person who forgets his past.
Cultural_Context: The proverb refers to the importance of the old and adherence to authentic heritage. He who has no old has no new. The basic principle is to keep what was as it was. A person must deal with the new without detaching himself from his values ​​and identity, combining the roots of authenticity with the data of modernity.

source_text: قلب الأم على الولد والولد قلبه على الحجر
english_translation: My heart for my son was broken, and my son’s heart for me was like a stone.
Cultural_Context: An indication of the mother's intense love for her children, and the children's lack of awareness of the extent of this love.

source_text: لا تسرف ولو من البحر تغرف.
english_translation: Constant dropping wears away a stone.
Cultural_Context: A proverb about a wasteful person who believes that what he has will never end. This proverb is famous in the Emirati society; to encourage balance in spending, and not to be wasteful, and it is in line with the Almighty’s saying: “and eat and drink, but waste not by extravagance” Surah Al-A’raf, 31. It is consistent with the noble Prophetic hadith: “Do not be wasteful with water, even if you are at a flowing river,” (authenticated by Al-Albani in the series of authentic hadiths).

source_text: لا في العير ولا في النفير.
english_translation: as useful as a chocolate teapot.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to describe useless people who do not play any role, belittles his status, and makes him seem insignificant among people. The originator of the proverb is Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, in order to belittle the status of the Banu Zuhra.

english_translation: Tomorrow is close if you wait it.
Cultural_Context: This means that the news that is hidden at the present time will appear with time, as the Levantine proverb says, “Tomorrow the snow will melt and the meadow will appear.”

english_translation: Grasp all, lose all.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said when there is a greedy person who does not satisfied for what Allah allotted for him.

source_text: من خاز عن داره قل مقداره
english_translation: East or west, home is best.
Cultural_Context: Call to cling to the land

english_translation: After black clouds, clear weather.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to highlight the importance of patience to achieve a goal.

english_translation: Comparing yourself to others only leads to sorrow.
Cultural_Context: This proverb conveys the idea that constantly watching and comparing oneself to others can lead to dissatisfaction, envy, and a lack of contentment, ultimately causing unhappiness.

english_translation: Greed is a nature.
Cultural_Context: A well-known proverb used to describe greed. It means that greed overwhelms a person’s heart and covers it, so he does not see the dangers that threaten him.

english_translation: All's well that ends well.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said to a person who has been away for a long time, and so people ask him about spoils and news. (ياب: bring), and the proverb is said to a person whose absence is prolonged or delayed, and it is a proverb is like the saying "the absent person has his excuse".

english_translation: Grasp all lose all.
Cultural_Context: A proverb that warns against the dangers of greed and avarice in societies and in dealings between people.

english_translation: Let sleeping dogs lie.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said about an unjust and tyrannical person because his sleep brings comfort and happiness to others, and because by distancing himself and sleeping he stops his troubles and evil from people, and therefore his sleep is like worship from which he and others reap great good.

english_translation: Don't live beyond your means.
Cultural_Context: It is used to express that a person must take into account his abilities, potential, and circumstances in all his actions in life so that he does not aspire to something that is not within the limits of his available capabilities.

english_translation: A flash in the pan.
Cultural_Context: العرج: The roots of the plant. The plant emerges from the depths of the earth to grow above the surface of the soil. The proverb is said of an obscure person who suddenly becomes famous.

english_translation: Old habits die hard.
