Cultural_Context: It expresses the difficulty of changing bad habits even after death, as their influence remains present despite changing circumstances or life experiences.

english_translation: You can't teach an old dog new tricks.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is used when someone is tasked with something that is too late or when someone tries to accustom another to something he is not used to. The proverb means that after he grew old and gray, they took him to school to learn.

english_translation: A falling master makes a standing servant. / It is a sorry house where the hens' crow and the cock is silent.
Cultural_Context: The proverb refers to the change of conditions and bad replaces good.

english_translation: your sins have caught up the flesh is week.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said to describe an abusive person who has gone too far in his abuse and thought that there would be no punishment or deterrent for him, and suddenly the strict and decisive punishment comes quickly.

source_text: أَجَت إِلْحَزِينَة تِفْرَح مَا لَقَتِلْهاش مَطْرَحٍ
english_translation: Born to suffer.
Cultural_Context: This popular proverb is used to express bad luck.

english_translation: He has kicked the bucket.
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to a person who has passed away.

source_text: أَسْمَعْ كَلامَكَ أصدقك، أشوف فَعَايْلَك/ أعمالك أسْتَعْجِب/ أستغرب
english_translation: Actions speak louder than words
Cultural_Context: The proverb indicates that the contradiction and hypocrisy between words and actions is a cause for astonishment or disapproval.

english_translation: he is the only boy on the beach.
Cultural_Context: The proverb describes mean people who consider words directed at them and causes problems.

english_translation: Out like a light.
Cultural_Context: The proverb refers to a person in a deep sleep.

english_translation: Take it easy.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is a call for simplicity and modesty.

english_translation: Absence makes the heart grow fonder.
Cultural_Context: This proverb highlights the theme that creating some distance or space can increase appreciation and affection.

source_text: إبعد عن الشر وغنيله، وهات فاس وقَني له.
english_translation: Wake not a sleeping lion
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that a person should not only move away from evil with all his might, but sing to it, so that it may pass safely.

english_translation: Like father, like son.
Cultural_Context: This proverb underscores the idea of benefiting from one's environment or family affairs.

source_text: إللي إيده بالمَي مش مثل إِللّي إيده بالنَّارِ
english_translation: Easier said than done.
Cultural_Context: This proverb means that people in comfortable or easy situations (like having their hand in water) cannot fully understand or relate to those who are in difficult or painful situations (like having their hand in fire). It emphasizes the idea that experiencing hardship or struggle provides a different perspective and understanding compared to those who have not faced such challenges.

english_translation: Talk of the devil, and he is sure to appear
Cultural_Context: This proverb means that if you are constantly afraid of something, you are more likely to encounter it or let that fear manifest in your life.

english_translation: More haste, less speed.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is used to encourage people to be patient when dealing with matters.

english_translation: No pain, no gain.
Cultural_Context: It means that achieving success or reaching a goal often requires hard work, effort, and sometimes discomfort or sacrifice.

source_text: اللي ما يطول العنب حامض عنه يقول
english_translation: They would find a fault with a fat goose.
Cultural_Context: It describes someone who was unable to achieve something and then denied it and spoke ill of it.

english_translation: Lucky is the one who is oppressed and not oppressor.
Cultural_Context: It is used to console the soul at the time of failure.

english_translation: like mother like daughter.
Cultural_Context: The proverb refers to the similarity of personalities between mother and daughter.

english_translation: Arrow often hits the shooter.
Cultural_Context: It has the same meaning of "He who dug a hole fell into it."

english_translation: Apples and oranges.
Cultural_Context: It is used to compare two different places or two opposite things (Zarqa and Balqa are Jordanian cities)

english_translation: Birds of a feather flock together.
Cultural_Context: It is said about those who agree on the baseness of their nature.

source_text: عتبها على أهلها من قلة عقلها.
english_translation: A bad workman always blames his tools.
Cultural_Context: The proverb describes a woman who is not resourceful.

source_text: فرعون فرعن من قلة ناس تضبه.
english_translation: There can be no tyrants where there are no slaves.
Cultural_Context: It describes someone who acts arrogantly because there is no one to stop him.

source_text: مش كل من صف الصواني حلواني
english_translation: Anyone can cook but not everyone can be a chef.
Cultural_Context: It is said to someone who does trivial work that does not benefit him.

source_text: يا داخل بين البصلة وقشرتها ما ينوبك إلا ريحتها.
english_translation: Don't go between the tree and the bark.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said when someone interferes in the affairs of others, to indicate that he will find something that will annoy him and spoil his mood.

source_text: أكلب الكدرة أعلى فمها الطفلة تتبع أمها
english_translation: Like mother, like daughter.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that the daughter always resembles the mother in her morals and behavior.

english_translation: If a job is worth doing, it's worth doing well.
Cultural_Context: Its meaning is similar to the noble hadith: “May Allah have mercy on whoever does a good deed and does it well.”

english_translation: A bad workman blames his tools.
Cultural_Context: It is used to describe someone who is ordered to do something he is not willing to do.

source_text: اشوف الشيبانِ الْتَاكِ مَا شَافْ آفِكْراشْ الْوَاكِفْ.
english_translation: An old dog is the best teacher.
Cultural_Context: It is important to take the opinion of the elderly as they have more experience.

english_translation: All things come to those who wait.
Cultural_Context: It means that whoever is patient will achieve all his wishes. "The shadow" is a metaphor for the fact that patience in the face of hardships is followed by relief.

english_translation: Do not spare anything in this life.
Cultural_Context: It is used to describe someone who spends from what God has given him easily and without stinginess.

english_translation: To break the ice.
Cultural_Context: It is used to describe the disappearance of reservations and the absence of barriers between people.

english_translation: Charity begins at home.
Cultural_Context: This proverb means that things are not lent when they are needed.

english_translation: Slow and steady wins the race.
Cultural_Context: It is used to encourage patience and not to rush.

english_translation: Man needs money for the evil day.
Cultural_Context: The equivalent is “A white dirham will benefit you in a rainy day.” The proverb refers to the benefits of saving and managing money well.

english_translation: He who serves leads.
Cultural_Context: It is equivalent to the proverb (A man’s servant is his master). The proverb is a call to humility and to avoid arrogance and conceit.

english_translation: It is never too old to learn.
Cultural_Context: The proverb has the same meaning as “Seek knowledge from the cradle to the grave,” and is a call to be scientifically curious, and an implicit prohibition against other types of intrusion.

english_translation: While you want to build, others want to tear down.
Cultural_Context: They use it as an example of someone who works hard to serve someone else's interests and wants the best for him, while the other person works hard to spite him.

english_translation: What goes around comes around.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that the world is like loans, because the borrower becomes poor one time and becomes rich the next.

english_translation: Too much ado about nothing.
Cultural_Context: It is used to describe something that scares you but is not dangerous. The equivalent in classical Arabic is "The mountain suffered labor and gave birth to a mouse."

source_text: العين الا تخطات حاجبها أخسر واجبها
english_translation: Too much of a good thing is bad.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that if something goes beyond its limits, it will turn into its opposite.

english_translation: let bygones be bygones.
Cultural_Context: The proverb urges not to look back and regret what has passed.

english_translation: People who don’t walk in your shoes can’t understand your journey.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is used to urge not to rely on someone who does not share your expectations of what might happen.

english_translation: A burden shared is a burden halved.
Cultural_Context: This proverb means that cooperation makes things easier.

source_text: دِرْهَمْ في الكف أُلاميَّ في اتْلَفْ
english_translation: Better an egg today than a hen tomorrow.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that a little is better than a lot that is not guaranteed to be obtained.

english_translation: Good things come to those who wait.
Cultural_Context: Maybe it will be better for you to wait.

english_translation: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
Cultural_Context: It is said to express a mother's love for her children, who sees no fault in them, even if people see the opposite.

english_translation: After a storm comes a calm.
Cultural_Context: No love except after enmity

english_translation: strike while the iron is hot.
Cultural_Context: It means "strike while the iron is hot", and the proverb is a call to seize good opportunities, and to be quick-witted and act quickly.

source_text: العين الا تخطات حاجبها أخسر واجبها
english_translation: Abundance, like want, ruins many.
Cultural_Context: The meaning of the proverb is clear: if something goes too far, it will turn into its opposite.

source_text: أَجَت الحَزِينة تِفرَح ما لاَقَتَش لهَا مِطرَح.
english_translation: Born to suffer.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used for someone who is unlucky or mismanages things and does not anticipate the consequences of things. The story of the proverb: There was a village in Palestine where the people used to marry their sons in groups and at one time of the year, especially in the summer months, when the nights are moonlit. There was an engaged spinster woman, and she agreed to marry with the group, but when the wedding night approached, the village headman discovered about her marriage and rejected it completely, since marriage is only for young men and virgins, while the bride cried from her bad luck and said the aforementioned proverb.

english_translation: He took the lion's share
Cultural_Context: A similar proverb: "He who is first is the one who ate the jujubes." This proverb means that the one who is first is the one who took the good of something, and only the less valuable remains. The story of the proverb: It is known that the grape harvest season in the Levant is in August. In June, a thief went to steal grapes from a nearby vineyard, when the grapes were unripe, and were still salty in taste. He did not like their taste, and left them for his colleague to pick, who took the raw grapes (the unripe grapes). The next day, when his steal was discovered, he mentioned his colleague and said (He took the grapes and left me the unripe grapes), and this became a popular proverb that is passed down through the generations. This proverb is said when the latecomer finds nothing but leftovers. A similar proverb: "He left the party without having Hommos."

source_text: اذا لَم تَكُن فَارِسًا كُنتَ الفَرِيسَة
english_translation: Strike the first blow. / DO OR DIE.
Cultural_Context: The proverb encourages courage and respect, as there is no place in this world for the submissive who will be coveted by other powers. This proverb applies to our present age; the age of strength, knowledge, values ​​and morals. Messenger of Allah (PBUH) said, "A strong believer is better and dearer to Allah than a weak one, and both are good".

english_translation: A bribe works miracles. / A dog will not cry if you beat him with a bone.
Cultural_Context: This proverb encourages generosity and liberality, as honoring and celebrating a guest are authentic Arab traits. Of course, returning a favor and acknowledging it are two traits that are the opposite of generosity, as kindness can only be met with kindness. (The eye is ashamed): a person is ashamed and returns the favor. This proverb does not mean seeking to offer a bribe, which is a reprehensible trait that we must not help and prevent because it corrupts peoples and nations, and bribery has never spread in a nation without destroying it and taking it away.

english_translation: He laughs best who laughs last.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to indicate patience and deliberation, as he who laughs last laughs the most.

source_text: الجَمَل لو شَاف عوَجَة رقبته ما انعَوَج عن الناس
english_translation: The pot calling the kettle black.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used for someone who describes people based on their faults.

english_translation: We're all in the same boat.
Cultural_Context: It is usually used for misfortunes and calamities, or to indicate that the need is the same, and one person cannot help another, as the circumstances are the same, and the one who does not have something cannot give it. This proverb is used for consolation, as everyone is waiting for Allah's mercy and provision.

english_translation: There's no such thing as a free lunch.
Cultural_Context: Al-Heday: The Kite, a type of bird of prey that flies high in the sky. The proverb is from the environment, as the kite lives in rural areas where there are chicks, rabbits and chickens. The proverb means that bad things only come from other bad things, as the kite cannot leave a chick it has kidnapped easily and will rush to eat it or pass it on to its children before it is gone. This proverb is used for someone who gets something and no one can take it from him easily.

source_text: الخُنِفسَانِة شَافَت ابنَها على الحِيط قالت: يسلَم لِي بَيَاضَك على سَوادِ الحيط.
english_translation: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
Cultural_Context: A beetle is a dark black insect that lives at the edges of houses and in the open areas. It can sneak into houses and walk on walls easily. This beetle once saw her little son walking on the wall and she got confused, thinking he was the white one and the whole wall was black. So she said her famous saying. This proverb is used for someone who considers what he does to be the best and right, unlike what others do. It is similar to this proverb: "No one sees his oil cloudy."

english_translation: Out with the old, in with the new.
Cultural_Context: It is said to someone who has a bad habit and advises him on how to give it up.

english_translation: People in glass houses should not throw stones.
Cultural_Context: Jeering: It is to mention a person's faults face to face and in front of his friends, and women usually use this method. A person may Jeer another person for the same thing or shame that exists in him, and this is one of the very vile methods. The poet said: Do not forbid a behavior and then do the same... Shame on you if you do it is great. This proverb is used for someone who Jeers persons for faults he already has.

english_translation: A falling master makes a standing servant.
Cultural_Context: The gazelle and the monkey are fast and active animals, but there is a big difference between them in appearance. The gazelle is well-known and the monkey is well-known, and when the gazelle is replaced by the monkey, it will be a great loss. This proverb is used when the beautiful is replaced by the ugly.

english_translation: A burnt child dreads the fire.
Cultural_Context: It is said when a person is let down and becomes cautious after it is too late.

english_translation: Neither fish nor fowl.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means "I leave you the honey, bee, so leave you alone and do not sting me." This proverb is used to avoid the evil of someone when it is clear that they are harmful, so it is better not to approach them and to be careful. The proverb also indicates that there is no smoke without fire, so whoever wants to pick honey, must be stung by some of the bees that made the honey.

source_text: بيَاكُل ما بيشبَع وبيخَرفُوه ما بيِسمَع.
english_translation: A hungry stomach has no ears.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used for a fool who is not fit for ransom or sacrifice, i.e. he does not meet the conditions. If he does not feel full, he is not rational. It is said (When stomachs are hungry, the hearts in the chests go blind). It is said: (If hunger were a man, I would have killed him) / or (If poverty were a man, I would have killed him).

source_text: بِيت الاَسَد ما بِيخلَي مِن العظَام
english_translation: A leopard can't change its spots.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used for someone who is generous and then time wrongs him. Like a lion's den, there are still some bones left after the prey, so the house of a generous and chivalrous person has some remains. It is said that the son of Hatim al-Ta'i had a guest as a guest who was an acquaintance of his father, who was the most generous of the Arabs. However, he had passed away some time ago and the guest did not know about of his death. Son of Hatim al-Ta'i was poor and his father did not leave him anything. The son put his hand on his head and began to think until sleep overcame him. While he was sleeping, he saw his father's hand shaking him and his father saying to him: "Come to me to take the gifts of your guest." Son of Hatim al-Ta'i woke up and went to his father's grave and found a camel kneeling on the grave that had abandoned the caravan. He took it and slaughtered it for his guests and family. It was said that Hatim al-Ta'i honored his guests even though he was dead, May Allah have mercy on him and reward him with good.

english_translation: When the going gets tough, the tough get going.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used when things are difficult, then suddenly become easier for a simple reason that was not expected, especially if a sick person uses most of the medicines to treat him, but he may be cured with a very simple medicine, and if you know the cause, it is easy to treat. There is a verse that says: Every illness has a cure except stupidity, it stupefies he who tries.

english_translation: Buy a pig in a poke.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said when someone sells to another a product that he has not seen, or the seller does not want to show it to him, or he may promise to show it to him later, and asks him to set a specific price for it. Just as you cannot sell or buy fish while it is in the sea, you cannot buy something without seeing it and evaluating it. This proverb is used when you are wanted to express your opinion on something that you have not tried or seen.

english_translation: United we stand, divided we fall.
Cultural_Context: It is an example to encourage cooperation and solidarity.

english_translation: Union is strength.
Cultural_Context: The union makes it easier to get things done efficiently.

english_translation: There is safety in numbers.
Cultural_Context: A proverb used to encourage unity in the face of injustice.

english_translation: Many hands make light work.
Cultural_Context: It means that the only way to accomplish great burdens is to work together. This is a proverb that is used to encourage cooperation, to distribute the burden among all members of the group.

english_translation: Go big or go home.
Cultural_Context: A proverb that calls for honoring people and generosity.

english_translation: In unity there is strength.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that strength comes from cooperation and solidarity.

english_translation: Together we are stronger.
Cultural_Context: The proverb suggests that a weak person can defeat a strong person if he finds help from someone else.

english_translation: Strength in numbers.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that the more people involved in completing a task, the faster it will be completed.

english_translation: Blood is thicker than water.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that kinship encourages relatives to help each other.

english_translation: Speak of the devil.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used when the conversation is about someone, and he/she appears during this conversation, or shortly after. Another proverb may be said for this occasion, “May you live long.” This proverb may also mean that there is no need to mention a person’s bad deeds without providing evidence of them, so that the person has the opportunity to defend himself. Mentioning of the dog here is because a dog may bite and stab if it encounters a person who is not armed with a stick, or anything to defend himself, and so that it can be used to attack the dog if it is present.

english_translation: Well-known like wildfire.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said to refer to someone who is so famous and well-known that people know him more than the fires that rise up the mountains and that everyone knows.

english_translation: Experience is the best teacher.
Cultural_Context: It means exaggerating the preference of the experienced person over the doctor, and some correct the narration of the proverb by saying: “Ask the experienced person and do not forget the doctor.” The first proverb is the one common between people.

source_text: إصرف ما في الجيب يأتيك ما في الغيب.
english_translation: Spend money to make money.
Cultural_Context: A proverb encourages spending money, and Allah will grant you from where you do not expect. Pocket: a bag sewn into clothing to carry money and so on.

english_translation: A beggar with a Havana.
Cultural_Context: Al-Nazhi: A person who enjoys walking and having fun. Usually, only well-mannered, pampered young men have these qualities, not those who have faults. The proverb is used for someone who puts himself in the wrong place and ignores his own faults.

english_translation: A friend in need is a friend indeed.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that a true friend is the one who supports you when you face difficulties and problems in life.

english_translation: Any port in a storm.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that a person in a predicament will look for any solution or help, even if it is not enough or does not provide the final solution to his problem, to get out of the predicament.

english_translation: make a mountain out of a molehill.
Cultural_Context: The proverb describes anyone who exaggerates things that are not worth exaggerating, according to the speaker's point of view.

english_translation: Nothing lasts forever.
Cultural_Context: It means that things cannot remain the same without change.

english_translation: Better a moment of pain than a lifetime of suffering.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that it is better for a person to endure the pain of treatment than to endure the pain of a long illness. The proverb is similar to: “The pain is only an hour, but the wonder is long.”

source_text: أنا باللقمة لفمو وهو بالمشهاب لعيني.
english_translation: Biting the hand that feeds him.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to describe a person who is ungrateful and betrays others.

source_text: إذا تخلطت الأديان شد في دينك
english_translation: Stand firm in your own convictions.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used when a person is confused and is advised to stick to his principles and ideas.

source_text: اسمع للراي اللي يبكيك ولا تسمع للراي اللي يضحكك
english_translation: Better to be slapped with the truth than kissed with a lie. / Bitter truth than sweet lies.
Cultural_Context: The proverb points out the importance of benefiting from honest and useful advice even if it is painful, rather than being attracted to opinions that may be fake or unhelpful and that may seem fun or comforting but may lead to dire consequences.

source_text: الباب إلى يجيك منو الريح سدو واستريح
english_translation: If you are always dwelling in trouble change the address.
Cultural_Context: The wind means troubles, problems and difficulties, and as long as its door is open, it will continue to hit you from every side. Sometimes we forget to describe this door and the type of problems it brings, so the suffering and pain last longer.

english_translation: A cheerful look makes a dish a feast
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that what the person you love gives you is of great value to you.

english_translation: Trouble never comes alone
Cultural_Context: (The house is open, and the wife is crazy). It is said when disasters befall a person, and he cannot bear the misery any longer than he is in, and this happens in the worst of circumstances.

source_text: الذي خرج من داره قل مقداره
english_translation: east or west, home is best.
Cultural_Context: A person who leaves his home loses his value.

english_translation: A fair-weather friend.
Cultural_Context: A friend who you do not know his intention.

english_translation: There is an excess of familiarity at the root of all hostilities.
Cultural_Context: When a person feels hatred towards another person and cannot confront him, he tries to show what is in his heart by saying it through joking.

english_translation: Two birds with one stone
Cultural_Context: The proverb is used to describe the combination of two good things.

english_translation: A soft answer turns away wrath
Cultural_Context: A kind word comforts and pleases, even if it is a compliment.

english_translation: Fight fire with fire.
Cultural_Context: These proverbs convey the idea of responding to wrongdoing with an equally strong or even stronger response.

source_text: اللي بغات الزين تضرب على تخراق الوذنن
english_translation: He who gathers honey, must suffer the stings
Cultural_Context: Those who want to adorn themselves must endure their piercing to wear earrings.

english_translation: Grasp all, lose all
Cultural_Context: It means that a person who aspires to have everything without compromising anything may end up losing everything.

english_translation: Bad company corrupts good character
Cultural_Context: "Qudra": A pot used to cook food that may leave behind residue or blackness. The proverb suggests that being close to something or someone bad can make you affected or similar to them, even if you don't intend to.

source_text: اللي عضو الحنش يخاف من الحبل
english_translation:
Once bitten twice shy.
A burnt child dreads the fire
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that whoever is harmed by something fears everything similar to that thing, and all the circumstances of that situation that frightened him or caused him loss.

source_text: اللي عندو الساقية يشرب من ماها
english_translation: Take benefit from what you have
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that whoever has a resource or means to achieve his goal can benefit from it directly.

english_translation: We lost all what we have done
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that the work or effort put into something was in vain or did not achieve the desired results.

source_text: اللي ما رضى خببزة يرضى بنصها
english_translation: Half a loaf is better than no bread
Cultural_Context: It is an example of a person who is not satisfied with what God has destinied for him and is forced to accept less in the end.

source_text: اللي ما عندو فلوس كلامو مسوس
english_translation: A poor man’s tale cannot be heard
Cultural_Context: It means that someone who has no money, “his words are inaudible and worthless (like food without salt).”

english_translation: What must be, must be
Cultural_Context: What Allah has destined for you is what will happen and there is no escape from it.

english_translation: True love comes from the heart, not from coercion.
Cultural_Context: This means that love is not forced and should be true and deep from the heart.

source_text: المرا بلا والد، كالخيمة بلا وتاد
english_translation: Sons are old age shelter
Cultural_Context: The proverb refers to the importance of children in a woman's life, and compares a woman who does not have children to a tent that lacks a peg, which is the pole that holds the tent together and enhances its stability.

source_text: المرا تخاف من الشيب كيف النعجة تخاف من الديب
english_translation: Woman fears age
Cultural_Context: It expresses that a woman is afraid of gray hair (age) as a sheep is afraid of a wolf.

english_translation: Looks can be deceiving.
Cultural_Context: Many proverbs and popular sayings range from wisdom to sarcasm and even guide people on how to judge people or events with insight and reason.

english_translation: He who depends on others' wealth is always poor.
Cultural_Context: This proverb applies to anyone who takes possession of someone else's property to enjoy it and be proud of it, but sooner or later it will be taken away from him. The proverb advises us to be content with what is rightfully ours.

source_text: الهدرة بين اثنين والثالث بلا وذنين
english_translation: Don't poke your nose into others' affairs.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that if there is a conversation between two people, the third party should not interfere in between them to know what they are saying. This proverb is said to a curious person who wants to know everything, including things that do not concern him.

source_text: الي فاتو زمانو ما يطمع في زمان الناس
english_translation: Act your age, not your shoe size.
Cultural_Context: This proverb expresses that an old man should not act like younger people, as this is not appropriate for him. He cannot imitate them, as each generation has different ideas and behaviors from the next generation. When the elderly try to imitate young people, they appear inappropriate. They should appreciate their age and the stage they have reached.

source_text: بات في الغيظ ولا تبات في الندامة
english_translation: It is better to be in safe than sorry
Cultural_Context: When a person suppresses his anger in his chest, he will suffer a lot, but that is much easier than a person committing a foolishness that costs him dearly and he regrets it when regret is of no use to him.

english_translation: go along with a liar
Cultural_Context: The proverb indicates that a liar cannot continue to deceive others for long, and that he will eventually expose himself.

source_text: جارك القريب خير من خوك البعيد
english_translation: Give a hand to the nearest
Cultural_Context: It means that a close neighbor who lives next door to you and shares your daily life can be more connected than a distant sibling who may be distant physically or emotionally.

source_text: جوز على الواد الهادر ولا تجوز على الواد الساكت.
english_translation: Cross the loud river but don’t cross the silent one".
Cultural_Context: The proverb suggests that dealing with a person who expresses himself clearly is more straightforward and easier to solve problems with than a person who does not speak and does not clarify his problems.

english_translation: A friend is someone who shares your happiness and your pains.
Cultural_Context: It means that the real person who loves you is the one who shares all aspects of your life with you, whether in happy times (joy) or difficult times (sorrow).

english_translation: East or west, home is the best
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that a person would rather endure personal pain or harm than be exposed to circumstances that would lead to losing or being separated from his homeland.

english_translation: Cunning as a fox.
Cultural_Context: He is very evasive and cunning and uses tricks.

english_translation: Don't brag about yourself let others praise you
Cultural_Context: It is said to someone who praises and thanks himself as a form of bullying.

english_translation: My hands are tied
Cultural_Context: The proverb is used to describe everything a person desires but cannot do or achieve.

english_translation: A secret for two, soon a secret for nobody "
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that a secret known by only two people can become known to thousands of people.

english_translation: like mother, like daughter
Cultural_Context: The proverb expresses the importance of noticing the family manners when choosing a life partner. It means that the mother's assessment, or the parents' character, in general, can be an indicator of how children will be raised and their characteristics.

english_translation: The effort is big, but the reward none
Cultural_Context: Used to indicate a great deal of effort or a long wait, which ends in little or no result.

english_translation: Birds of feather flock together
Cultural_Context: The proverb is used to express the compatibility between two things.

english_translation: Empty vessels make the most noise.
Cultural_Context: The proverb expresses someone who boasts about his knowledge of all things that do not concern him or his work and appears ignorant in front of people.

source_text: عدو عاقل خير من صاحب جاهل.
english_translation: A sensible enemy is better than a narrow-minded friend
Cultural_Context: It suggests that a wise adversary can be more manageable or less harmful compared to a foolish friend who might cause problems due to their lack of knowledge or insight.

english_translation: I taught him to swim he tried to drawn me.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to express that a weak person is robbed and treated unjustly by people.

source_text: قول كلام الخير ولا اسكت خير
english_translation: Speak kindly or refrain from talking.
Cultural_Context: The proverb encourages using positive and beneficial language and advises against saying anything that could be hurtful or unnecessary.

english_translation: Look before you leap.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means you should assess and think things through carefully before making a decision or taking action.

english_translation: Good things come to those who wait.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that every setback or delay may have a hidden benefit or positive outcome. It suggests that what might initially seem like a negative situation could actually bring about good results or valuable lessons in the end.

source_text: كل خنفوس في عين امه غزال
english_translation: The beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
Cultural_Context: It means that people tend to view their loved ones or those they cherish in an idealized or exaggerated way, regardless of their actual qualities.

source_text: كي نشوف هم الناس ننسا همي.
english_translation: When I think of the other’s misfortunes, I forget mine."
Cultural_Context: That means when I get tired of life and see poor and miserable people, I forget my problems and thank god for that.

english_translation: The one who shows his fears ensures his salvation.
Cultural_Context: That means don't involved in dangerous situations to stay safe.

source_text: مالقاوش في الذهب عيب قالو كي يلمع يوجع العينين
english_translation: One would find a fault with a fat goose.
Cultural_Context: It highlights how people sometimes seek flaws or criticize even the most beautiful things, just for the sake of criticism.

english_translation: A man is known by the company he keeps
Cultural_Context: One of the popular proverbs that people use, which includes an urging to avoid bad company and seek the company of good people.

english_translation: All that glitters is not gold.
Cultural_Context: It means that not everything that looks good or appealing is truly valuable or useful.

source_text: هرَبْت من قطّاع الرّيوس طحت في وكّال ابن آدم
english_translation: Out of the frying pan into the fire.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said about a person who flees from bad and falls into worse.

source_text: وقيّة زهر خير من قنطار فهامة
english_translation: Better to be lucky than smart.
Cultural_Context: Arabs believe so much in luck as a factor of success in life that they put it before an individual's self-worth. It highlight the importance of luck or chance in achieving success, sometimes even more than intelligence or ability.

english_translation: A fool's errand.
Cultural_Context: A proverb used to mock and despise a person’s actions or condition in front of others.

english_translation: It takes two to tango.
Cultural_Context: The proverb highlights the importance of collaboration and the need for joint efforts to achieve goals.

source_text: يربى فم الجرح، ما يربى فم العار
english_translation: Many words hurt more than swords
Cultural_Context: It is used to criticize hurtful and influential words that leave their mark for years, unlike the wound that only takes a few days to heal.

english_translation: Sleeping with one eye open.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said to indicate a person's cunning and deceit.

english_translation: There's no getting away from me.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said as a threat to take revenge on the aggressor.

source_text: إذا في خير، ما كان تركه الطير.
english_translation: Good things don't get left behind.
Cultural_Context: It means that things that others do not need is of no benefit or use to you.

source_text: إذن من طين وإذن من عجين.
english_translation: Turn deaf ear.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said to describe the careless people who do not listen to the advice and guidance of others.

source_text: ابن الحرام بيساويها وابن الحلال بيوقع فيها
english_translation: Sometimes the innocent suffer with the guilty.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that the innocent person always bears the mistakes and consequences of what the guilty person does.

english_translation: The apple doesn't fall far from the tree.
Cultural_Context: The wolf will only be a fierce and harmful wolf when it grows up. This proverb is said to someone who tries to change a person’s inherent character or traits.

english_translation: It's like a circus.
Cultural_Context: The literal meaning of the proverb is that in battle, those who throw spears and those who shoot arrows mix, and the proverb is used figuratively to express crowding, noise, and the rapid mixing of things together.

english_translation: in the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king
Cultural_Context: A bad person looks good compared to someone worse than him.

english_translation: Knowing yourself is the beginning of all wisdom.
Cultural_Context: Man is the most knowledgeable of all people about what harms and hurts him, and he is the most capable of protecting himself.

english_translation: Rome wasn't built in a day.
Cultural_Context: The proverb urges patience and not to rush into a matter or work.

english_translation: The proof of the pudding is in the eating.
Cultural_Context: It is a famous proverb in the Levant and Egypt as well, and it means that the test shows the truth of the statements and claims, and it is similar to the proverb that says: They told him the soldier is jumping over the wall, they were told this soldier and this wall.

english_translation: The shoemaker's wife is ill shod
Cultural_Context: The proverb describes someone who provides services to others, helps them, and does not help himself.

english_translation: Better suffer ill, than do ill.
Cultural_Context: It is better to be oppressed than to be an oppressor. The proverb urges avoiding oppressing people.

english_translation: Gift horse in the mouth.
Cultural_Context: It is said about something that a person obtains without effort or hard work.

source_text: بدّه من الدواق رطل وأربع واق
english_translation: Give him an inch and he take a mile.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said of the greedy person who is never satisfied and wants more in everything.

english_translation: The path to success is paved with difficulty.
Cultural_Context: A proverb for someone who does not reach his goal except after effort, suffering and torment.

english_translation: One bad apple spoils the whole bunch.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that one bad friend can spoil the rest.

source_text: تغدّى فيه قبل ما يتعشّى فيك
english_translation: Get your blow in first.
Cultural_Context: Attack him before he attacks you.

source_text: تيتي تيتي متل ما رحتي متل ما جيتي
english_translation: Came back empty-handed.
Cultural_Context: A proverb to express failure to change something or fulfill a need. It is said when one fails in his endeavor.

english_translation: A lie has no legs.
Cultural_Context: One of the famous popular proverbs that indicates that lies are quickly exposed and can never be hidden. This proverb is also famous in all the countries of the Levant and in Egypt.

english_translation: Putting lipstick on a pig.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to describe an ugly woman who is not helped by beautification.

english_translation: birds of a feather flock together.
Cultural_Context: One of the famous Syrian proverbs, it is said when two peopl with similar in character, behavior, and thinking, agree in something, whether they are right or wrong, good or bad. The equivalent of this proverb in classical Arabic is the proverb: “A can agreed with its plate.”

english_translation: Hungry enough to eat a horse.
Cultural_Context: It is said to indicate great hunger.

english_translation: As like a two peas in a pod.
Cultural_Context: A proverb is used to describe a strong relationship between two people or a similarity between two people.

english_translation: Too many cooks spoil the broth
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said when opinions differ on how to implement something.

english_translation: More money, more problems.
Cultural_Context: The proverb reflects the idea that money does not always guarantee happiness or peace of mind, but may bring with it challenges and anxiety.

english_translation: All roads lead to Rome.
Cultural_Context: In this context, the mill refers to the inevitable end result so the proverb means that no matter how different the methods and means used, the end result will remain the same.

english_translation: Forbidden fruit is sweet.
Cultural_Context: This proverb reflects how prohibitions can make people seek out what is forbidden even more, because of the attraction that the prohibition gives to the matter.

english_translation: Every problem has a solution.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used so that no one will despair, no matter what the problems are. There is no problem without a solution. Rather, there is someone who can solve it, and the faithful person is the one who leaves the solution to his problems to God. The proverb may be used to praise the intelligence of someone who is able to solve the problem.

english_translation: We're on the same page.
Cultural_Context: The word (passion) is metaphorical and means (we are all equal in this matter).

english_translation: There is no smoke without fire.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that there must be a reason or truth behind rumors or speculations that talk about someone or something in a negative way.

english_translation: When pigs fly!
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said about someone who falsely and slanderously demands what is not his right, using all means, even if they are despicable, to achieve his goal and desire.

english_translation: a drug on the market.
Cultural_Context: It is used to express the large number of women and girls for those who want to marry.

english_translation: Let bygones be bygones.
Cultural_Context: A traditional proverb that expresses tolerance and forgetting the past. It is concerned with the meaning of not paying attention to the past and regretting what has passed.

english_translation: in the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king
Cultural_Context: The bad one looks good compared to worse.

english_translation: They would find a fault with a fat goose.
Cultural_Context: It means that the person who cannot climb to pick grapes claims that he does not want to because they are not ripe (sour). The proverb is used to describe someone who is unable to obtain something and claims that he does not want it.

english_translation: Your sins have caught up with you
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said to describe an abusive person who has gone too far in his abuse and thought that there would be no punishment or deterrent for him, and suddenly the strict and decisive punishment comes quickly.

source_text: اجفي الجرّة على ثمها والبنية على ذيل أمها
english_translation: Like mother like daughter
Cultural_Context: It is said that a girl should follow her mother's morals.

english_translation: Gild the lily.
Cultural_Context: It is said when one person is unable to help another solve a problem, and may even make the problem more complicated.

english_translation: Good things come to those who wait.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to describe long-term patience in order to achieve one's goal.

source_text: اكسر البصله واشتمّها والبنيه على ذيل أمها
english_translation: Like mother like daughter.
Cultural_Context: It is said that the girl imitates her mother's character.

english_translation: The absent party is not faulty.
Cultural_Context: It is used to mean not rushing to hold someone accountable until he arrives and know the reason for his delay.

english_translation: A drowing man will catch at a straw.
Cultural_Context:
The origins of the proverb: (The drowning man clings to every grass) / (The drowning man leans on straw), the latter was common among the common people of Egypt in the eleventh century AH and (The drowning man clings to the grass) was common among the common people of Baghdad in the thirteenth century AH.
This proverb means that the drowning man tries to cling to anything he finds, even if it is grass floating on the surface of the water, or to cling to the tails of his clothes, thinking that these attempts will save him from drowning, but his desperate attempts do him no good.

english_translation: Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said to express a mother's love for her children, as she does not see any faults in them, even if people see the opposite.

source_text: اللي تلدغة الحية يخاف من جرد الحبل.
english_translation: Once bitten, twice shy.
Cultural_Context: Anyone who has been betrayed is afraid of everything around him.

source_text: الما يعرف يرگص يگول الگاع عوجة.
english_translation: Poor craftsman blames his tools.
Cultural_Context: People who can't finish their work successfully blame things around them. (He who can't dance says the floor is upside down.)

english_translation: Forgiveness is the attribute of the strong. / To err is human, to forgive is divine
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that the one who forgives, pardons, and overlooks the mistakes of others has generous qualities, because they are praiseworthy qualities that a person possesses.

source_text: الي ما یلوح العنب یگول حامض
english_translation: He/ She would find a fault with a fat goose.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that if someone is unable to reach the grapes on the tree because he is short, ill, or anything else, he will claim that the grapes are sour to justify his failure and preserve his pride.

english_translation: One half of the world doesn’t know how the other half lives.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used when a person is judged by the appearance of things and ignores their reality.

english_translation: A cat has nine lives.
Cultural_Context: It is said about the one who is always safe from misfortunes that he is like a cat that has seven lives.

source_text: تيتي تيتي مثل ما رحتي جيتي.
english_translation: Came empty-handed.
Cultural_Context: It means we went and came back as we left, without any benefit or achievement.

source_text: رجع أيد من وره وأيد من كدام
english_translation: Came away empty-handed.
Cultural_Context: Indicates that the person has returned without making any profit.

english_translation: The pot calling the kettle black.
Cultural_Context: The story of the proverb: It is said that two crows had a quarrel and met each other, so they began to jeer each other, and each one of them jeered the other for the blackness of its face, not knowing that both of them have black faces, but rather believed that the blackness was on the face of the crow facing it because it did not see its own face. There was a third crow was listening to this jeering, so it told them that both of them are black, and this saying became a proverb. It is used for those with bad character jeer each other.

source_text: كل ما جاله يمشي ليوره مثل بول البعير
english_translation: One step forward, two steps back.
Cultural_Context: It is said about a failed person that he continues to decline in his work.

source_text: لا تبيع السمجه و هيه بلشط
english_translation: Don't sell the skin before you've caught the bear.
Cultural_Context: Do not sell something that you do not yet own; it is like a fish that you cannot sell until you have caught it and it is still in the river.

english_translation: Fire could leave ashes behind.
Cultural_Context: A good father may have bad children, just as fire leaves ashes

english_translation: Between a rock and a hard place.
Cultural_Context: It is said about a person who cannot disclose his problem to avoid scandal that he is like someone who swallowed a knife, which will hurt him in both cases if he wanted to spit it out or continue swallowing it.

english_translation: All flesh is not venison
Cultural_Context: A proverb is used to describe something that is difficult to obtain.

english_translation: A burnt child dreads the fire.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to describe a person who exploits poor people to carry out several failed experiments.

english_translation: Eats like a pig.
Cultural_Context: Depicting a person who has a strong appetite for food, and mocking him.

source_text: أبوه بصل وأمه توم، ومنين بدها تجي الريحة الطيبة
english_translation: The apple doesn't fall far from the tree.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that nature prevails over nurture, that whoever resembles his father is not wronged, and that (the blame is not on you, but on those who raised you), and on the environment and upbringing in which you were raised.

english_translation: Devoured everything
Cultural_Context: The proverb refers to a gluttonous and very greedy person.

source_text: أكلا عَ بارد المستريح (أو باردة، أو عَ البارد).
english_translation: Lucky breaks.
Cultural_Context: These proverbs capture the idea of ​​achieving success or obtaining something with little or no effort, often due to luck or favorable circumstances.

english_translation: Blood is thicker than water.
Cultural_Context: The proverb expresses the strength of the bonds of relations between relatives and blood ties and blood ties will inevitably prevent the spread of enmity and the severing of relations between them no matter what happened.

english_translation: Buy a pig in a poke.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said when someone sells to another a product that he has not seen, or the seller does not want to show it to him, or he may promise to show it to him later, and asks him to set a specific price for it. Just as you cannot sell or buy fish while it is in the sea, you cannot buy something without seeing it and evaluating it. This proverb is used when you are wanted to express your opinion on something that you have not tried or seen.

english_translation: Absence makes the heart grow fonder
Cultural_Context: The distance or absence can enhance the value or sweetness of the person or thing in the eyes of others.

english_translation: a jinx on the house
Cultural_Context: This phrase is said to refer to the unlucky people.

source_text: يلي بيتو من زاز ما بيرشيء الناس حجارة.
english_translation: People who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones
Cultural_Context: He who lives in a glass house should not throw stones.

english_translation: A stitch in time saves nine.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is san equivalent to "prevention is worth a pound of cure" and suggests the necessity of sleeping in a warm place to maintain a good health and avoid illness.

english_translation: Don't put the cart before the horse.
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to someone seeks luxuries while he does not have the basics and necessities of life.

english_translation: Filling tummy and spending money.
Cultural_Context: The proverb describes a person who does nothing but eat and sleep, and is said about a lazy person, and is used to denounce unemployment.

source_text: ألمزوق من برا أشخبارك من داخل؟
english_translation: All that glitters is not gold.
Cultural_Context: It is used sarcastically when a person sees something that has a beautiful appearance but ugly inside.

english_translation: You can tell a book from its cover.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to argue that the cleanliness and condition of a place from the inside is evident from what it looks like from the outside.

source_text: إيلا كان حبيبك عسل، لاتلعقوش كامل.
english_translation: Don’t abuse the kindness of a friend.
Cultural_Context: This proverb urges maintaining a good relationship with the people you love and not to try to exploit their kindness and appreciation for you.

source_text: اشتري العقار من وارث ملاقيه ولا تشتريه من مالك بانيه.
english_translation: Something for nothing.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said to someone who wants to get something from someone else easily without tiring himself out.

source_text: اصبر لكل مصيبة وتجلًّدِ واعلم بأن الدهر غير مُخَلدِ.
english_translation: Good things come to those who wait.
Cultural_Context: This proverb urges patience in the face of adversity.

english_translation: Don't cry over spilled milk.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to advise someone to stop crying over what they have missed.

english_translation: Speech is of time, silence is of eternity.
Cultural_Context: The proverb discusses that silence is better than talking no matter how nice is it.

english_translation: A life for a life.
Cultural_Context: The proverb suggests that when an injustice or crime is committed, the appropriate punishment should be equal to the injustice committed. The origin of this concept can be traced back to ancient Arab law and religious teachings in Islam and some other ancient cultures.

source_text: الفقيه اللي عملناه إقابل الجامع عاد فالحصاير طامع.
english_translation: Give him an inch and he'll take a mile.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said about a person you thought well of, but he deserves you to think badly of him.

english_translation: Let he who is without sin cast the first stone.
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to the woman who criticizes people even though she has many flaws, like an ugly woman (Kuka) who criticizes someone a one-eyed woman.

english_translation: Think before you speak.
Cultural_Context: This proverb urges being caution and think wisely before talking.

source_text: اللي أمه في الدار قرصه حار.
english_translation: A mother's love is the best care.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that whoever has a mother who takes care of himis better off than others who have not.

source_text: اللي رجله في المويه ما هو زي اللي رجله في النار
english_translation: It's easier to give advice than to take it.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that a person who is in a safe situation cannot truly understand or feel the suffering or difficulty of someone who is in a serious problem or danger.

source_text: اللي ما يطول العنب حامضًا عنه يقول.
english_translation: Sour grapes.
Cultural_Context: It is said to justify failure to obtain something.

english_translation: A greedy man is always in want.
Cultural_Context: This proverb discusses the greed, as greedy people never be satisfied.

english_translation: A black sheep of the family.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to describe people who do not observe noble values ​​and customs, unlike their parents who were well-known for them and had a high social status among people.

source_text: امدح صاحبك مع الناس، ولومو الراس فالراس.
english_translation: Praise publicly, criticize privately.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to illustrate the necessity of supporting a friend in the among strangers, never blaming him for anything, and reprimanding him secretly.

english_translation: A cheerful look makes a dish a feast
Cultural_Context: The proverb is a clear expression that if someone you love give you an onion, you will consider it as a sheep.

source_text: تحلف لي أصدقك أشوف افعالك استعجب
english_translation: Better to see something once than to hear about it a thousand times.
Cultural_Context: The proverb refers to the contradiction and hypocrisy between words and actions as a source of astonishment or disapproval.

english_translation: Happiness is contagious.
Cultural_Context: This proverb indicates that a happy neighbor or friend spreads happiness to those around him.

source_text: جيت نعاونو فقبر باه هرب لي بالفاس.
english_translation: Bite the hand that feeds him.
Cultural_Context: It is said to someone who helped you but he wronged you.

english_translation: Half a loaf is better than none.
Cultural_Context: It is better to work for little or no pay than to remain unemployed.

english_translation: The best is yet to come.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used for someone who missed out on something that was not destinied, and perhaps good things are coming. It contains optimism about the future, and is like a hope that the coming things will be better.

english_translation: A leopard can't change its spots.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used for people who insists to commit fault for many times, despite promising not committing them again.

source_text: شْحَال مَا طَالْ اللِّيلْ كَيْطْلَعْ النّهار.
english_translation: The darkest hour is just before the dawn.
Cultural_Context: A proverb that expresses optimism and hope.

english_translation: Strike while the iron is hot
Cultural_Context: This proverb emphasizes the importance of taking advantage of opportunities while they are available before losing them.

english_translation: The die is cast.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said to a person who has a problem that he cannot get rid of.

english_translation: You get what you pay for.
Cultural_Context: If you buy something cheap, know that you will find half of it spoiled.

english_translation: Cutting off one's nose to spite one's face.
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to people who attempt to harm others through their actions, but in fact, they end up harming themselves more than anyone else.

english_translation: A bull in a china shop.
Cultural_Context: The proverb describes the ignorant person with a strong body. This proverb is used to describe individuals who act forcefully in situations where such force will not be useful, due to poor judgment or a lack of understanding of the situation.

english_translation: He who goes out in search of wool often comes home shorn.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to describe a person who returns to their family after a long absence in search of benefit, but instead of bringing something positive, they bring something harmful or detrimental.

source_text: قرصه في ناره وعينه على جاره.
english_translation: The grass is always greener on the other side
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to the greed that may affect a person, which makes him greed to have what others have, without being content with his own livelihood.

english_translation: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
Cultural_Context: It means that great things start small.

english_translation: She dug her own grave.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to describe a woman who has caused herself to be exposed and bad talk has spread about her.

english_translation: Consistency is the key to success.
Cultural_Context: The proverb indicates that it is about consistency, not quantity.

english_translation: You see the world as you are.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that every person looks at others and judges them according to what is in his heart and his own intentions. The bad person sees all people as bad like him, while the good person sees all people as good like him.

source_text: لا تشري حتى تقلب ولا تصاحب حتى تجرب.
english_translation: Look before you leap.
Cultural_Context: The proverb emphasizes the importance of caution when making a purchase. It advises to thoroughly inspect and verify the product before buying. Additionally, it suggests being cautious about associating with individuals until you confirm their honesty and integrity.

source_text: لا ينقل أخبارك إلا من داخل دارك.
english_translation: Beware of Greeks bearing gifts.
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to being careful about who enters your home and not trusting anyone.

source_text: لاشفت خطاها كبار فعرف انها رباضة.
english_translation: All talk and no action.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said to someone who says something he does not do.

english_translation: Stay in your lane.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that a person should act according to their abilities, circumstances, and statusand not acting pretentiouslyn.

english_translation: Use your head, not your heart.
Cultural_Context: One should not give in to every desire but should think and control their passions.

english_translation: Strength lies in forgiveness.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is used to indicate that someone in a position of power should forgive and show mercy towards the weaker or defeated individuals.

english_translation: Listen to your elders' advice.
Cultural_Context: The proverb highlights the importance of respecting and valuing elders or people who are more experienced in life. These people provide us with valuable experiences and lessons.

english_translation: A candle for God, a stump for the devil.
Cultural_Context: This proverb urges preventing backbiting and being keen on honesty and giving advice, no matter how harsh it is.

english_translation: He is a phony.
Cultural_Context: It refers to a person whose talks in useless matters and a chatterbox from whom no benefit can be expected.

english_translation: You cannot tempt providence and always triumph. / Don't push your luck.
Cultural_Context: This proverb urges cautious and not to be negligent, based on previous successful experiences in the same matter.

english_translation: A real dog.
Cultural_Context: The proverb refers to the person who has no value, whose presence is not considered.

english_translation: Show me your friends and I'll tell you who you are.
Cultural_Context: Individuals are influenced and imitated by their friends.

english_translation: He flies off the handle
Cultural_Context: The proverb is used to describe a person who is quick to anger, who becomes furious at the slightest thing that happens to him for any reason.

english_translation: Makes a fuss over nothing.
Cultural_Context: It is said about someone who always complains without any reason.

english_translation: Too many cooks spoil the broth.
Cultural_Context: Too many different opinions spoil the work. It's an equivalent for the saying: Too many hands in treatment will ruin it.

english_translation: Out of the frying pan and into the fire.
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to someone who goes home to rest from the hardships of work, but finds his home is full of problems.

source_text: أنا واخي على ابن عمي، وأنا وابن عمي على الغريب.
english_translation: Blood is thicker than water.
Cultural_Context: This proverb shows that personal interest comes before the public interest, and that a person prefers himself over others. A person supports his brother against his cousin, as he is closer than his cousin, and he supports his cousin against the stranger people, as he is closer to him. This proverb shows that a person must care for his family and support them against those who oppose them, as the closest relatives are more deserving of kindness, so he should take priority.

english_translation: A burnt child dreads the fire.
Cultural_Context: This proverb means that people do not care about someone who has no support and treat him like a testing ground.

english_translation: Haste makes waste.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said to describe patience and the success pf the patient people.

english_translation: You get what you pay for.
Cultural_Context: Al-Aal: The good thing. The proverb means that a good commodity is known by its price.

english_translation: The apple does not fall far from the tree.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that nature prevails over nurture, that whoever resembles his father is not wronged, and that (the blame is not on you, but on those who raised you), and on the environment and upbringing in which you were raised.

english_translation: A rose among thorns.
Cultural_Context: It is a popular proverb describes a woman who is as beautiful as the moonlight.

english_translation: The shoemaker's wife is ill shod
Cultural_Context: People say this proverb to mock some people who are unable to do a certain thing for themselves, but they do the same thing and master it for others.

english_translation: Beauty is only skin deep.
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to a man who decides to marry a beautiful and charming woman, but he does not care about her morals and behavior.

english_translation: Climbing the ladder of success by stepping on others.
Cultural_Context: The proverb refers to people who succeed through the efforts of others.

english_translation: Spend and god will send.
Cultural_Context: One of the famous Hadrami proverbs. “Khazaq”: Spend. This proverb has the same meaning of the famous popular proverb “Spend money and what is unseen will come to you”, which is a kind of encouragement to trust in God and that God is the provider.

source_text: ذا جيت بلاد العوران صيرن عين
english_translation: When in Rome, do as the Romans do.
Cultural_Context: One of Al-Sharaf and Sirwah proverbs. It is used to urge people to adapt to the customs of those they live with and follow their approach.

english_translation: Bold as brass.
Cultural_Context: A proverb used to describe someone who makes a mistake and tries to defend the mistake.

english_translation: If you don't ask, you don't get.
Cultural_Context: If someone needs anything he will be persistent and hasty in fulfilling it, and when fulfilling it depends on Allah’s will, he makes efforts to pray and insists on his need, waiting for his hope to be fulfilled immediately.

source_text: عز القبيلي بلاده ولو تجرع وباها
english_translation: East or west home is the best.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is applied to the homeland, as it is the real pride of a person, no matter how difficult life is in it, or no matter how hard life is suffered in it.

source_text: عيش رجب ترى عجب / أطلب عمر تنظر عجب
english_translation: Who lives, sees much.
Cultural_Context: Ask for more life to see more wonders.

source_text: فرس بني مخاشي يعرف طريق حوره
english_translation: The locals know best.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is very similar to the famous Arabic proverb, “The people of Mecca know their valleys best.”

english_translation: Face your fears.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that approaching the places of fear is enough to remove fears.

english_translation: His mouth is writing checks his body can't cash.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to describe people who talk more than they act.

english_translation: Don’t give a fool a tool.
Cultural_Context: The proverb urges not to give a crazy person a tool to work with when you know he is crazy.

source_text: ما يخمج الماء إلاّ خس البقر.
english_translation: Don't burn your bridges behind you.
Cultural_Context: The proverb means that the mean cow stirs up the water and makes it cloudy, so that other women cannot drink it. The proverb also means that the vile people disrupt the serenity of others’ lives or their relationships with each other.

english_translation: You can't have your cake and eat it too.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said for the person who wants everything at the same time.

english_translation: you are an empty suit.
Cultural_Context: Al-Makhlos: The naked perso. This proverb refers to the untrustworthy and useless person.

english_translation: Speak of the devil and he will appear.
Cultural_Context: This proverb refers to a person who seeks troubles that will cause him a lot of inconvenience.

source_text: من قارب الحداد يصبر على الشرار
english_translation: If you lie down with dogs, you’ll get up with fleas.
Cultural_Context: It is an equivalent for the famous Arabic proverb: “Whoever lives with a blacksmith will be burned by his fire” or “Whoever plays with fire will burn his fingers.”

source_text: نصح ياثور وها هي على قرنك
english_translation: The shortest distance between two points is a straight line.
Cultural_Context: It has a close meaning to the popular proverb, "Where is your ear, Juha?"

english_translation: Greed is the root of all evil.
Cultural_Context: This proverb indicates that greed has bad endings, and the greedy person will harm himself.

source_text: يدي في فمه واصبعه في عيني.
english_translation: Biting the hand that feeds him.
Cultural_Context: "My hand in his mouth": I am feeding him. "His finger in my eye": a metaphor for boasting, so it is said when someone is ungrateful.

source_text: البيض اللى وقع على بيض فقشه.
english_translation: The rotten apple injures its neighbour.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to indicate that a weak person reveals his true nature if he meets a weak person like him.

source_text: اللى فات الفوت ما ينفع الصوت.
english_translation: Grasp all, lose all.
Cultural_Context: It is said about someone who regrets something that has passed and it is too late.

english_translation: Spill the beans
Cultural_Context: It is said about a slanderer or gossiper who does not keep a secret and spreads it among people.

english_translation: Talking out of both sides of one's mouth.
Cultural_Context: It is said of the hypocrite who says something to you and another thing behind your back.

english_translation: Trust, but verify.
Cultural_Context: Some people do not keep their valuables in a safe place at home, and when they lose anything, they immediately accuse the servants and those closest to them. This is one of the common mistakes that occur in many homes. This proverb is said when valuables are lost and those close to them are accused of stealing them.

source_text: إذا زاد الشيء عن حده انقلب ضده
english_translation: Too much of a good thing is a bad thing.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said to encourage moderation and not to go to extremes, and therefore it is said (neither excess nor neglect).

source_text: الباب اللي ايجيك منه الريح سده واستريح
english_translation: If you are always dwelling in trouble change the address.
Cultural_Context: It is said to someone who complains about a problem with clear causes. It is also said when a person fears a someone who causes problems, so he has no choice but to stay away from him or cut off his relationship with him.

english_translation: Half a loaf is better than no bread.
Cultural_Context: This proverb urges satisfaction, and it refers to be content with the simple things, as this is better than losing everything.

english_translation: Preaching to the choir.
Cultural_Context: It is used to mock someone who brags while he is surrounded by his family and being protected by them.

english_translation: Like father like son.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said about someone who resembles one of his parents in appearance and character.

english_translation: No pain, no gain.
Cultural_Context: It is said to the novice trader who wants quick profit and cannot bear loss and limited profit.

source_text: اللي ياكل على ضرسه يشبع نفسه
english_translation: Every man for himself.
Cultural_Context: When a person is in a good health and relies on himself in having food, he will benefits from this food, which positively affects their health, and vice versa. The proverb is used to describe someone who relies on themselves in any task, succeeds, and does not depend on others.

english_translation: Too many cooks spoil the broth.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said when a company is closed due to the mismanagement of its owners and their dependence on each other to manage it.

english_translation: gild the lily.
Cultural_Context: A proverb used to describe an inexperienced person who tries to fix something and then ruins it.

english_translation: Words with no actions.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said about someone who talks a lot but does little.

source_text: حد تعرفه ولا احد ا تخبط فيه
english_translation: Better the devil you know
Cultural_Context: A proverb is said when someone advises you to replace an employee or worker you know with another one you do not know.

english_translation: Cut from the same cloth.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said to encourage marriage between relatives, and it is also said to put the right thing in the right place.

english_translation: keep your nose out of other people's business.
Cultural_Context: The proverb encourages not interfering in a problem that does not concern you, and just watching it from afar.

english_translation: keep him in the dark
Cultural_Context: If a person is an expert in a certain field and works in it, and he sees a competitor doing the same work but not performing it as required, then here the expert is not required to intervene to guide and help, as letting the person stumble blindly in his work is better for him and more appropriate so that he does not come as a competitor to him in the future. The proverb is said to urge not to give advice to a competitor in work.

english_translation: An ape’s an ape a varlet’s a varlet; though they be clad in silk or scarlet.
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said when nature overcomes nurture.

english_translation: A flash in a pan.
Cultural_Context: It is a proverb when an unqualified person says something or makes a good statement and it is credited to him.

english_translation: A narrow margin
Cultural_Context: There is a longitudinal line on the top edge of the ship. If sea water reaches it, this means that the ship is in danger and on the verge of sinking. This proverb is used to describe a person who reaches difficult and late stages in everything. It is said when a person with limited income is asked about his living conditions, whether they are good or not.

english_translation: flog a dead horse
Cultural_Context: The proverb is said to someone who is given advice many times but does not care.

english_translation:
All is not gold that glitters All. 
Fine feathers do not make fine birds
Cultural_Context: The proverb describes a man who wears luxurious white clothes, but his house is black with filth.

source_text: أن جادت عليك بخيط العنكبوت تنقاد وان حرنت تقطع سلسل الحداد
english_translation: you win some you lose some.
Cultural_Context: It is said about the world, as if it is easy for you, you will be led by a spider's thread because of its extremely weak, and if it opposes you, the largest chains will be cut, and this is the world.

source_text: إن ضاق بيك الأمر، اشرب زجاجة خمر
english_translation: Let them drink and forget their poverty and remember their misery no more.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is widely used by the Ja'aliyin, Kawahla, Khawalda, and Arkaiyin in the Wad Madani region (according to the author), and the proverb is religiously, medically, scientifically, and logically rejected as well.

english_translation: In for a penny, in for a pound.
Cultural_Context: Literally, it means that if you are unable to fill a hole, you should widen it. This means that if you are indebted to many creditors, and you are unable to pay, you should increase spending.

source_text: اب سن يضحك على اب سنين
english_translation: People in glass houses should not throw stones.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is said to someone who makes fun of someone has more faults than him.

source_text: ابن العبدة منه الخير جبدة، ومنه الشر يبدا.
english_translation: You cannot gather grapes from thorns, nor figs from thistles
Cultural_Context: There is a similar proverb: "The servant's son is mean."

source_text: اسمع كلام الكبير و لو كان
english_translation: Older than you by a day, wiser than you by a year
Cultural_Context: Listen to the elderly, even if they are not rich, powerful, or influential, because their experiences are not without authority.

english_translation: Turn a blind eye.
Cultural_Context: This proverb is used to describe people who ignore people’s words, or in other words (who are ignorant).

english_translation: Don't confuse me with facts!
Cultural_Context: It is said to someone who disagrees with something clear and evident. It is said to him, “I tell you it is abull", and you say “Milk it”! It is known that a bull does not give milk.

english_translation: Charity begins at home
Cultural_Context: This means that charity work must start at home, as the Egyptian proverb says: “If the oil is not enough for the family, it is forbidden for the neighbors.”

english_translation: you made your bed, now you have to lie in it.
Cultural_Context: It is used to describe anyone who has caused a disaster or something to himself and cannot control what he has done or is beyond his control.

english_translation: What goes around comes around.
Cultural_Context: This is a Sudanese proverb that is often used to describe someone who does something and it backfires on them, even after a while. There was a man who owned a goat. He had a (Qard) tree, which is a jujube tree that grows naturally and is widely spread in different regions of Sudan. This Qard tree was planted in the courtyard of the house. The goat ate a large amount of the saffron from the Qard tree and got tired from eating so much saffron, and its belly swelled until it was close to death. Before it died, its owner slaughtered it, skinned it, and tanned its hide with Qard so that it would become (fur). The proverb means that the goat brought evil upon itself. Therefore, it became a custom and people began to use this proverb and use it on different occasions to describe people who bring trouble upon themselves.

english_translation: Remove an old tree and it will wither to death.
Cultural_Context: This proverb indicates the continuity of misery throughout the life of the miserable person.

english_translation: When the tree is fallen, every one runs to it with his axe.
Cultural_Context: This proverb means that any criminal who falls into a disaster is gloated over a lot, and there is a lot of talk that he caused problems, so he was likened to the fallen bull.

english_translation: What is meant to be will always find its way.
Cultural_Context: What is meant for you must happen to you.

source_text: الحسنه في المنعول شي الشره في القندول.
english_translation: For every good deed comes evil.
Cultural_Context: It means that there is no good in someone who has no hope.

english_translation: Better to be alone than in a bad company.
Cultural_Context: In Sudan, the word “Fasl” means a stingy, and “Khalaa” means the wilderness and desert. The overall meaning of the proverb: It is better for a person to walk in the wilderness and desert alone, rather than being with a stingy friend.

english_translation: In the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king.
Cultural_Context: Meaning a man with little education in a country or region whose people are ignorant is like a scholar to them, so it is said (the one-eyed man in the land of the blind is a king).

english_translation: You cannot teach an old dog new trick.
